essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: EXASPERATION: PERSONAL BACKGROUND AND EARLY CAREER

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: Paek Kyŏnghae was born in 1765 into the Suwŏn Paek family, which had resided in Chŏngju, Pyŏngan Province, for many generations, ever since his ancestor Paek Yŏk had moved to the area in the dynastic transition period from Koryŏ (918–1392) to Chosŏn. The Suwŏn Paek family of Chŏngju had formed one of the most prominent lineages in Chŏngju, producing 25 of Chŏngjus 282 higher civil service examination (munkwa) passers and building tight marriage ties with regionally renowned lineages. For example, Paeks mother was a descendant of No Yŏlchi (born in 1633, passed munkwa in 1663, Hamjong magistrate, Jr.3) of the Haeju No of Chŏngju, a lineage that produced eighteen successful munkwa candidates. Paek Kyŏnghae himself married a Papyŏng Yun of Kasan, a member of a powerful lineage that produced nine munkwa passers. His two sons married a Yŏnan Kim and a Paechŏn Cho, respectively, members of the two most successful descent groups of Chŏngju in terms of producing munkwa passers. Like other yangban families throughout the Chosŏn period, the illustrious lineages of Chŏngju and nearby districts secured their prestigious positions as ruling elites in local society by negotiating close marriage alliances among themselves.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: Paek Kyŏnghae began his studies in 1770, at the age of five, when his father, Paek Sŏnyang, opened a village school on the sunny slopes of Mt. Kadŏk and invited a teacher, Hwagok, to instruct his sons. It was Hwagok, along with Songdam—Paeks remote relative but the leading figure of his lineage because of his success in the 1756 munkwa and subsequent official career—who became the most esteemed role models in Paeks life. Paeks own talent was recognized early, for it is known that he was able to discuss the Analects (論語) at fourteen. When Paek took the munkwa in 1786, at the age of twenty-one, the examiners assumed that he must be a man of Yŏngnam and a disciple of Toegye or Hoejae, the two most prominent Neo-Confucian scholars of the Chosŏn, because his scholarly performance at the examination was excellent. The examiners were greatly disturbed after learning of Paeks regional background—a reaction that proved to be an unfortunate prelude to the ups and downs of Paeks subsequent career.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: Indeed, despite such an outstanding performance at the examination, Paek was assigned to the Royal Academy (Sŏnggyungwan 成均館) as a trainee, like other successful candidates from the northern provinces, because the court discriminated against northern residents from the moment they passed the examination. As noted by Chŏng Yagyong (1762–1836), a distinguished scholar of the late Chosŏn period, the successful candidates from prestigious lineages (chŏngjok 淸族) were given apprenticeships in the Office of Diplomatic Correspondence (Sŭngmunwŏn 承文院), whereas northern residents were assigned to train at the Royal Academy, and secondary sons of yangban at the Office of Editorial Review (Kyosŏgwan 校書館). Military examination passers were also treated differently, in that their first jobs were assigned in accordance with their social backgrounds. Only those who were from notable yangban lineages were given prestigious positions at the Office of Transmission (Sŏnjŏngwanchŏng 宣傳官廳), via which they could be promoted to higher offices. Those with less prestigious family backgrounds were given positions at the Office of Patrol (Pujangchŏng 部將廳) or the Gatekeepers Office (Sumunjangchŏng 守門將廳). This differential treatment of successful exam candidates according to their family backgrounds did not emerge until some time in the mid-Chosŏn. According to Yi Ik (1681–1763), another prominent scholar, in the early Chosŏn period successful examination candidates were divided into a few groups according to age and talent, and then placed in different offices (pungwan 分館). By Yi Iks time, however, this initial assignment system had been transformed into a very hierarchical one that gave preferential treatment to prestigious yangban families (pŏryŏl 閥閱).

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: In 1788, two years after Paek earned the munkwa degree, he received his first position, as Third Proctor at the Royal Academy (Sŏnggyungwan Hagyu 學諭, Jr.9), and he concurrently served as Administrator of the Bureau of Superannuation (Kiroso Sujik 耆老所守直). As table 1 shows, his career looked quite promising in his early years at court, for he was appointed Temporary Recorder of the Royal Secretariat (Sŭngjŏngwŏn Ka-chusŏ 承政院假注書), a senior seventh-rank position, almost immediately after he began his official career. A little more than one year later, he was promoted to Assistant Section Chief of the Ministry of Rites (Yejo Chwarang 禮曹佐郞, Sr.6) and concurrently held the position of Recorder (Chusŏ), both reputable senior sixth-rank positions in the Chosŏn court hierarchy.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: During the Chosŏn period, some positions, such as the chŏngjik 淸職 (prestigious offices) or chŏnghwan 淸宦 in the central government, were regarded as more prestigious than others because they involved serving the king in physical proximity to him, required great scholarship, and involved matters of personnel and remonstrance. Examples of these offices were mid- to low-level positions in the censorate offices and the offices in charge of recording and writing documents, including the Office of the Censor-General (Saganwŏn 司諫院), the Office of the Inspector-General (Sahŏnbu 司憲府), the Office of the Special Counselors (Hongmungwan 弘文館), and the Office of Royal Decrees (Yemungwan 藝文館). The Director of the Office of Transmission (Sŏnjŏngwan) in the military ranks also belonged to this category. The yojik 要職 (reputable posts) was another category of prestigious positions in the court hierarchy. Section Chief (Chŏngnang 正郎) and Assistant Section Chief (Chwarang) in the six ministries belonged to this class.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: One way to preserve the integrity of these prestigious offices was to control the process of selecting officials. For most offices, either the Ministry of Personnel or Ministry of War submitted a list of three candidates to the king, who then made the final choice by placing a dot by the appropriate name. In contrast, current officials in the Office of Special Counselors selected the candidates for positions in that office, by marking a circle (kwŏnjŏm 圈點) by the candidates name. After the censorial offices reviewed this roster of successful candidates (Hongmunrok 弘文錄), state councilors with second rank or higher, the Director of the Office of Special Counselors, and officials with senior third rank and above (tangsanggwan 堂上官, Sr.1–Sr.3) at the Ministry of Personnel met to examine the qualifications (hoegwŏn 會圈) of each candidate. The final roster (Todangnok 都堂錄) was then presented to the king, who appointed officials according to the grade that each candidate earned. Similar steps were taken to select officials for the Office of Royal Decrees.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: These measures were originally designed to ensure that only talented and qualified people held prestigious positions in the government. However, they soon became a useful way to screen family and factional backgrounds when selecting candidates for these prominent positions that, once secured, guaranteed further advancement up the ladder of bureaucratic success. Two social groups—secondary sons of yangban and residents of the northern provinces—continuously lodged complaints against this discriminatory and exclusive appointment system. Unrelenting efforts to unlock this system by secondary sons of yangban resulted in a series of reforms that gradually allowed them to take the civil service examinations, to hold yojik (reputable posts), and, finally, to hold chŏngjik (prestigious positions) as well (beginning in 1772). Northerners and their sympathizers also appealed to the court on numerous occasions to rectify the unfair appointment and promotion systems. These appeals often resulted in orders from the king to resolve the issue in their favor. For both secondary sons and northerners, however, the reality of discriminatory practices continued until the end of the dynasty, despite legal revisions and royal efforts to undo the injustices of the appointment system.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: It is not surprising, therefore, that Paek underwent many ordeals during his official career since he was from one of the northern provinces. An incident of 1789, when he was a Recorder, is illuminating. On the twenty-second day of the second lunar month, there was much business to take care of, but Paek brilliantly carried out his job of recording court sessions and reading memorials aloud, which involved simultaneous translation and interpretation from Korean into literary Chinese and from literary Chinese into Korean. Thus King Chŏngjo (r. 1776–1800) asked which lineage the Recorder came from. Not knowing the answer, Second State Councilor Yi Sŏngwŏn asked Paek. Paek answered, I belong to the lineage of Previous Third Inspector of the Office of Inspector-General (Sahŏnbu Changnyŏng) Paek Inhwan. After hearing this, the king said, Then you are not a descendant of Hyuam Paek Ingŏl. (Paek Ingŏl was also a member of the Suwŏn Paek lineage but belonged to a different branch that flourished in the south.) Third State Councilor Chae Chegong then commented, How could a person from a remote place know about Hyuam? The king asked, Who is this Paek Inhwan? The Minister of Taxes, Sŏ Yurin, answered, He is the one who served in offices of prestigious positions years ago. The king said, This Recorder passed the exam and his literary talent is really prominent. Then Chae replied sarcastically, That is not the real nature of a person from a remote place (hato-chi-in 遐土之人).” The king, however, not only repeatedly praised Paeks talent, but also promoted him to Assistant Section Chief of the Ministry of Rites, ignoring these pointed comments from high ministers.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: This promotion was a coup for Paek, both because this position was one of the chŏngyojik (prestigious and reputable positions) and one rarely bestowed upon a person from Pyŏngan Province, and because it meant that he had been promoted to the chamsanggwan 參上官 (positions of rank six and above), a major hurdle for all members of the Chosŏn court as they advanced toward higher positions in the bureaucratic hierarchy. Yet he also had to face a censorate organs rebuff of his promotion on grounds of the rarity of a rustic person (hyanggok-chi-in 鄉曲之人) holding such a prestigious position. Probably under special protection provided by the king, Paek managed to assume the position of Assistant Section Chief.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: Nonetheless, the kings favor was not consistent. At the year-end evaluation of bureaucratic performances in 1789, although Paek received a high grade for his job performance, King Chŏngjo personally marked him low grade because he had been disobedient a few months before, and thereby dismissed him. In the ninth lunar month of 1789, the king had secretly invited Yi In (1755–1801), his half-brother, who had been accused of plotting treason and banished to Kanghwa Island, to the capital. The queen mother and many officials had disapproved of this and requested that the criminal be escorted back to Kanghwa Island. The kings response had been somewhat excessive, and Nam Hangmun, the Royal Secretary (Sŭngji 承旨), had refused to write it down. The king had then ordered Paek to announce his instructions, and Paek too disobeyed.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: Despite his disobedience, Paek was appointed Section Chief of the Ministry of Works (Kongjo 工曹 Chŏngnang, Sr.5), with a concurrent position of Historian (Kyŏmsa 兼史). This promotion was, however, followed by the demeaning royal admonition that the position of Kyŏmsa differed little from that of a eunuch (implying that he must thus be subservient to the king).

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: Yet Paek could not blindly follow royal orders when they violated proper norms and values. His second case of disobedience, which took place in the eleventh lunar month of 1790, also had to do with Yi In. Sin Kihyŏn had allegedly supported Yi Ins above-mentioned plot, and the queen mother instructed that he be banished. King Chŏngjo not only disapproved of official demands that Sin Kihyŏn be banished, but also wanted to appoint him Royal Secretary (Tongbusŭngji 同副承旨, Sr.3). Accordingly, he dismissed any official who could object to his decision and then ordered Paek to write the appointment letter. Despite repeated orders by the furious king, Paek did not obey because he believed to do so would be tantamount to abandoning the Confucian values he held as an upright, loyal subject. As a result, Paek was repeatedly scolded by the king and beaten as punishment. Eventually, he lost his position and furthermore did not receive any appointments for eleven years, between 1790 and 1801, except for a few months in 1794–1795 when he held the position of Section Chief of the Ministry of Rites (Yejo Chŏngnang).

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: One can argue that Paeks demotion in these two cases had less to do with his regional background than with court politics. Nonetheless, one should not overlook the fact that the court politics that the king tried to take advantage of at the time were closely tied to regional issues. According to Paek, the position of Kyŏmsa (Historian) had originally been one of the yojik, but from 1776 on it had been given to men from the countryside, and especially to those from Pyŏngan Province. This policy itself can be seen as one of the measures the king took to augment monarchical power and authority by hiring people previously marginalized from central political power. However, the original purpose did not seem to prevail, for the esteem in which Kyŏmsa were held had declined ever since the policy was adopted. Paek argues that the positions degradation had worsened because Kim Ponghyŏn (1732–?, munkwa in 1768) from Chŏngju had developed a very submissive attitude toward court ministers and had accepted abusive treatment from them during his service as a Kyŏmsa for many years. This had resulted not only in the aforementioned perception that those holding the position of Kyŏmsa were little more than eunuchs but also in the practice of deliberately humiliating Pyŏngan people.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: In the two cases in which Paek was disobedient, the king had apparently assumed that Paek would blindly follow orders because, being from Pyŏngan Province, his political fate by and large depended on the kings favor. Paeks defiant stance halted his official career at the center, but earned him the reputation of being an upright official and the respect of his fellow literati of Pyŏngan Province.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: ADVOCACYPaek Kyŏnghae seems to have developed a heightened regional consciousness during the eleven-year period (1790–1801) when he stayed in the countryside. In 1794, he visited the memorial hall (chŏngnyŏ 旌閭) dedicated to Yi Kyehyang of Yŏngbyŏn, one of four loyal subjects from the same family who had been killed during the Manchu invasions. During this visit, he witnessed the dilapidated condition of the memorial hall and deplored the fact that the court did not pay due attention to the descendants of this family because they were from Pyŏngan Province. On another occasion, he found an old engraving on a horse-shaped rock near the Kadŏk village school and ruins of residences to the northeast of the rock. He thought that these were remains from the Koguryŏ kingdom (?–668) and resented the fact that no documents existed from which to learn the regions ancient history. Paek also wrote of how his own teacher, Hwagok, had dissuaded Han Ungnok, a man from one of the prominent lineages in the region, from studying the Confucian classics in order to pass the munkwa on the grounds that men from Pyŏngan Province had no future in official careers.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: In 1802, after the long unemployment and bitter experience he had accumulated as a person from the Kwansŏ (關西) region, Paek wrote a Letter to the State Council on Behalf of Pyŏngan Residents. The letter primarily demands (1) ending differential traineeship assignment of munkwa passers according to their familial and regional backgrounds, and (2) allowing Pyŏngan residents to obtain prestigious positions (tongchŏng 通淸). It begins with a strong sense of pride in the regions three-thousand-year history. Paek points out that the Kwansŏ region was referred to as the small civilization (sohwa 小華) at the time of the legendary ancestors Tangun and Kija, and that during the Koguryŏ period it was known as one of the strongest states under Heaven. Thus, he argues, it was not a place abandoned from the beginning. He describes the area as having become a territory without master once the Tang dynasty defeated the Koguryŏ and it came to be used as a wild hunting ground by northern barbarians. Koryŏ officials had tried gradually to recover the territory, but it had been invaded by Khitans and Mongols. After the Chosŏn dynasty was founded, early kings concerned with the security of this area had selected wealthy and powerful families from the south to relocate there. Paek indicates that eight or nine of the regions ten great lineages had resulted from this relocation in the early Chosŏn period. He concludes that the Kwansŏ region was not a peculiar place from the beginning. The land belonged to Tangun and Kija, and the people are the people of this country.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: Worship of Kija and Tangun had become an integral part of Korean cultural identity by the late Chosŏn period. As early as the Three Kingdoms period, Kija had been recognized as the transmitter of civilization to Korea, but it was during the Chosŏn period that Kijas heritage was highlighted. From the beginning of the dynasty, the court declared its intention to resume the indigenous broken transmission of the Way originally implanted in Korea by Kija, as a measure to legitimize the founding of the new dynasty. Subsequently, Chosŏn intellectuals often regarded Kija as a great Confucian sage. It was in this early Chosŏn period that Tangun also came to be celebrated on a regular basis as the legendary progenitor of the Korean people. At that time, the court established a separate shrine for Tangun and Kija in Pyŏngyang, Pyŏngan Province, and began offering memorial services to them. Although the court was criticized for its negligence in maintaining these shrines, from this time on these two figures became tangible cultural symbols of the Chosŏn state.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: Along with many other people from Pyŏngan Province, Paek embraced such cultural symbols because they shared the same space as these two cultural heroes who had presumably established their rule there. Indeed, the regional identity that was part and parcel of the mind-set of the 1812 rebels, as shown in their rebel manifesto, was almost identical to that advocated by Paek Kyŏnghae in his letter to the State Council, since, for example, the rebels stressed the provinces significance as the founding place of Kija Chosŏn. Moreover, Confucian scholars and current and retired officials from Pyŏngan Province relied on the same rhetoric to promote regional alliances against the rebels. This strategy was illustrated in a circular (tongmun 通文) to organize volunteer units in the Pyŏngyang area, which invoked the names of Tangun and Kija in order to remind people that the province was the home of scholarship and propriety.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: In addition to discussing Pyŏngan Provinces historical identification as the birthplace of the Chosŏn dynasty, Paeks 1821 thesis on the original, correct sound of the Korean colloquial language discusses a unique cultural asset that the region had preserved. Paek points out that the sage King Sejong (r. 1418–1450) created the native alphabet and established the correct sound of the native language by gathering wise scholars and repeatedly consulting Ming Chinese scholars. He argues that King Sejong must have acknowledged the fact that Kwansŏ was the birthplace of Korean civilization and therefore adopted the sound of this region as the standard when he systemized the native language (pangŏn 方言). Since King Sejongs reign, however, the pronunciation of the native language has changed in other parts of the Chosŏn state. For example, the original sound tyŏn (텬) became chŏn (천), while ti (디) turned into chi (지). Thus the sound of tyŏn-ti (텬디; Heaven and Earth) changed to chŏn-chi (천지). Likewise, the sounds ta (다) and ta (타) became cha (자) and cha (차). While wondering why seven regions (excluding Kwansŏ) followed the same path of transformation in pronunciation, Paek emphasizes that the people of Kwansŏ still preserve the original, correct sound of the native language. He also refers to other evidence that establishes Kwansŏ as the original source of the correct sound of the native Korean language. For example, King Sukchong (r. 1674–1720) evidently had the same question in mind when he asked his officials which dialect was correct. A renowned official replied that it was that of Kwansŏ. Therefore, Paek triumphantly concludes, under Heaven, the sound of chunghwa (中華) is correct; in our eastern country, the sound of Kwansŏ is correct. Kwansŏ provided the basis of our eastern countrys language.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: This self-glorifying thesis also sheds light on how the Pyŏngan dialect—which Paek deemed to be original and correct, yet different and distinct from others—may well have provided non-Pyŏngan people with a foolproof tool for distinguishing Pyŏngan people. Paeks point is well taken precisely because the Pyŏngan dialect is distinctive, as Paek himself inadvertently exemplifies in his thesis. It is ironic that the linguistic preservation that Paek felt compelled to advertise turned out to be an all-too-effective way to discern regional background. More paradoxically, despite his pride in the linguistic originality of his region, Paeks orientation toward the center probably made him mimic the central dialect when needed. For example, it seems that Paek turned off his Pyŏngan accent when he took the oral components of the munkwa exam, since his examiners thought he must be either from the capital or from Kyŏngsang Province, as discussed earlier.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: At any rate, Paeks letter to the State Council continues with his resentment over regional discrimination. He opens his discussion with very general remarks, pointing out that When a father and eight sons [that is, the king and eight provinces] live together, their nobleness and baseness or thinness and fatness must be the same. He then discloses the essence of the discrimination against northerners in the employment of court officials, a view that he shared with Chŏng Yagyong: Civil officials [from Pyŏngan Province] are assigned only to the Royal Academy and military officials to the Gatekeepers Office. Even though one is a scholar who has mastered the Heavenly Principle and has unprecedented talent, one has no hope of advancement. Such political discrimination stirred public contempt, to the extent that “even toddlers who have just learned to speak already differentiate and insult people from Pyŏngan Province, and people of base status, pushing carts, arrogantly embrace such popular contempt toward Pyŏngan people. Everyone calls us sŏin 西人. Even worse, they call us sŏ-ji-han 西之漢.’ Paek cries out,

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: [They scorn us] as though Heaven does not cover us, Earth does not embrace us, the Sun and Moon do not shed their light upon us, and frost does not fall on us. [They do so as though] we are not human, we are not animal, either; they do not seem to know what kind of monster or ghost we are. It seems that nothing can be compared to us. Alas! What crimes have we sŏin committed? Are sŏin alone not endowed with the nature of yin-yang and the five elements? Is our speech completely incomprehensible, given that it is likened to that of the western barbarians? Are our caps and dresses so different and strange compared to those of other provinces? Does the land become despicable because of the people [living there], or do the people become despised because of the land? I have never heard, in the world under Heaven and Earth, that any [country] divides the land, looking down on a part of it and abandoning it for such a long time [and] to such a severe extent as this.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: Paek then seeks the origins of such regional contempt, which were all too bitterly humorous to him. Contrary to the conventional belief that political discrimination against Pyŏngan people had been prevalent from the beginning of the Chosŏn dynasty, Paek indicates that it began in the middle of the dynasty. He first acknowledges that, at the outset, the Chosŏn court did root out the coarseness of Silla and Koryŏ institutions and did not differentiate between remoteness and closeness, or between inner and outer regions, in the employment of officials. Therefore, he points out, in the early Chosŏn there were people from Pyŏngan Province whose appointments reached ministerial levels. Some became directors of the Royal Academy; others ran the Munwŏn 文苑 (Hongmungwan or Yemungwan), holding chŏngjik positions. According to Paek, it was only from the mid-dynastic period that the Pyŏngan people were blocked from obtaining chŏngjik. The story goes that a civil minister (munjae 文宰) who stayed in Pyŏngyang for a long time, as an escort of a Chinese envoy (Kwanbansa 館伴使, Sr.3), was bitterly criticized for his wild debauchery by a local Confucian scholar. The ministers frustration and hatred of the people of the area allegedly led to the initiation of regional prejudice and discrimination. The offending civil minister was Sŏ Seyang (1486–1562, munkwa in 1509), a powerful and talented scholar-official of the sixteenth century. In 1633, this episode was cited by Minister of Personnel Choe Myŏnggil as the origin of regional discrimination and was also recorded in a local gazetteer.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: Paek, however, does not blame any one person for triggering such political discrimination. He goes on to analyze three popular perceptions held at the time to justify political discrimination against people from Pyŏngan Province.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: 1. There Are No Yangban TherePaek comments that this first point is illogical and groundless. After defining yangban as high civil and military officials (yangbanja munmu kogwan chi ching ya 兩班者文武高官之稱也), he argues that it is not true that there have been no high military and civil officials from Pyŏngan over the past two hundred years. He names as examples Special Capital Magistrate (Uyun 右尹, Jr.2) Cho Changnae (1686–?, munkwa in 1715), Yangŭi-gong 襄毅公 Kim Kyŏngsŏ (1564–1624), and Yangmu-gong 襄武公 Chŏng Pongsu. Paek clearly resents the fact that their descendants had been unable to receive the same degree of honor given to people of similar family pedigrees from other provinces, and were discriminated against from the moment they entered the central bureaucracy. He concludes that should people from Pyŏngan Province be employed in the future, they should not be scorned under the pretext that there are no yangban there.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: Although Paek did name a few renowned officials from Pyŏngan Province, even he could not have denied that the number of scholars and officials from the region who had earned fame in the Chosŏn up until his time was embarrassingly small. In addition, since a proper familial background was crucial for being a yangban in the late Chosŏn, Paek and his colleagues from Pyŏngan Province were fighting a losing battle in terms of obtaining official recognition of their qualifications for chŏngjik. There is no doubt that by Paeks time the elite in Pyŏngan Province had successfully adopted mature yangban culture based on Neo-Confucian prescriptions. They pursued Confucian scholarship—the primary requirement needed to sit for the civil service examinations—and practiced Confucian rituals. They had resided in a set location from the early Chosŏn period on; had organized various Confucian local voluntary and independent institutions, such as community compacts (hyangyak 鄕約) and the local yangban roster (hyangan 鄕案), to realize their interests at the local level; and had formed tight, exclusive marriage networks among themselves. In a nutshell, the thorough cultural transformations of elite life in Pyŏngan Province by Paeks time were arguably comparable to those that had taken place in the south. Yet those cultural practices could not alter the family pedigrees of Paek and his fellow elite from Pyŏngan Province, and pedigree remained the most critical qualification for penetrating the thickly woven network of the central aristocracy, which almost monopolized high and prestigious positions in the central bureaucracy.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: 2. The Province Is Close to the Barbarian LandOn this second point, Paeks argument is creative and appealing. After reminding his readers that the Chosŏn state is close to the Wae 倭 (Japanese) to the east and the Ho 胡 (northern barbarians, or Manchus) to the north, he questions whether there are any differences between the Wae and the Ho in terms of their uncivilized nature. He then points out the inconsistency embedded in the popular perception that linked spatial proximity to barbarians to a coarse nature and unrefined culture. In other words, people scorned Pyŏngan Province because it was close to the Ho, yet they did not despise the Yŏngnam region (Kyŏngsang Province) despite its proximity to the Wae. Paek concludes that this discussion of proximity to the Ho is deceptive and unwarranted, a ploy to legitimize regional discrimination.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: In arguing about proximity to both the Wae and the Ho, Paek may have had more in mind than just physical and geographical space. Physical closeness entails material, cultural, and human contact, which can result in a mixture of blood and cultural influence. Recent experiences of direct contact in the form of the Japanese and Manchu invasions—which to the Chosŏn people represented their barbaric nature in its most extreme form—must have had a similar effect. Paek regarded the Japanese and Manchus as sharing a similar uncivilized nature, so it must have seemed cogent to him to argue that physical proximity to the Manchus alone could not be used as proof of the norths cultural vulgarity.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: Paeks worldview did not differ fundamentally from the China-centered culturalism (chunghwa sasang 中華思想) that Confucian literati upheld in the Chosŏn period. The ancient Zhou dynasty had been a symbol of chunghwa culturalism, and had thus been revered throughout history (chonju-ron 尊周論), although the legitimate holder of true Confucian civilization had changed successively over time. The essence of chunghwa theory was hwa-yi-ron (華夷論), hwa here referring to chunghwa, the successor of Confucian civilization, and yi referring to those barbarians who had not reaped the benefits of Confucian transformation and who thus relied only on naked power and force. The Chosŏn elite took pride in having been blessed with the transformative effects of Confucianism and promoted the Chosŏn state as eager participants in its civilized world. They developed this line of thinking into so-chunghwa 小中華 thought, in which the Chosŏn dynasty was viewed as a lesser but legitimate center of Confucian civilization. After the demise of the Ming, this sohwa consciousness developed even further, so that Chosŏn intellectuals believed that it was the Chosŏn that had inherited legitimate Confucian culture, and hence that it was their responsibility to defend this culture. Naturally, Paek borrowed the language of his contemporary Neo-Confucian literati to position the Chosŏn dynasty at the center of cultural discourse. Furthermore, he defended the northwestern region as a participant in this civilized sphere, and one that should not be stigmatized simply for its physical proximity to the uncivilized Ho.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: Paek himself demonstrated a balanced view of each regions cultural particularities, including his own. He later served, for about two and a half years, as Superintendent of Yugok Post Station (Yugok Chalbang 幽谷察訪, Jr.6) in Kyŏngsang Province, beginning in the seventh lunar month of 1804, and wrote an essay on the culture of Kyŏngsang region (嶺南風土). In it he gave high marks to the frugal lifestyle of the Kyŏngsang people, who emphasized propriety and scholarship. Nonetheless, he criticized them for rather blindly revering literary works left by previous scholars and tending to repeat useless discussions. He was also concerned about the wanton establishment of private academies in the area and about the united but arrogant attitude of the Yŏngnam elite, who insulted the magistrates and even disobeyed the kings orders. Pointing out that the people of the Kwansŏ region were divisive, short-tempered, and profligate, he concluded that it would be wonderful if the two provinces could learn from each other.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: 3. There Is No Scholarship TherePaek constructs an elaborate argument against the third popularly held bias, that there was a lack of scholarship in Pyŏngan Province. He acknowledges that the people of Pyŏngan were ashamed of their less prominent scholarly achievements, but maintains that such shame only came from their own modesty. After pointing out that there was no special breed of people who became great ministers or generals in the beginning, he asks whether there can be no one who is endowed with the right forces of Heaven and Earth in the forty-two districts of Pyŏngan. Paek adds what he had heard from elders—namely, that early Chosŏn kings had never discriminated against people from the periphery, nor had provincial and district administrators uttered the word sŏto with contempt. Instead, they had established schools and had encouraged proper decorum to lay the foundation for respecting ones superiors and being willing to die for ones elders. People of the region had also not considered themselves, as sŏin, to be objects of contempt. Therefore, people had often exerted themselves, caught others attention, and been recommended to the court. Such people included Tunam Sŏnu Hyŏp, Hwang Chibam of Pyŏngyang, Pak Hapkang of Sŏngchŏn, Han Chŏngan of Sunan, and Yun Sŏngpa and Yun Chwiam, a father and son from Yŏngbyŏn. All had been from Pyŏngan Province and had comprehended the truth, learned from their mentors, and achieved illustrious scholarship.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: As Paek tries to prove, Neo-Confucianism began to spread in Pyŏngan Province as early as the sixteenth century, when Chungam Cho Hŏn (1544–92), who held the position of the Preceptor (Kyosu 敎授) in Chŏngju, laid the foundation of Confucian learning in the area. Kim Sangyong (1561–1637), who had once served as the magistrate of Chŏngju, was generally remembered as the one who had greatly promoted Confucianism. Two other magistrates, Maeng Sehyŏng and Maeng Chusŏ, were also known to have disseminated Confucian teachings to young scholars in the area. Inhyŏn sŏwŏn, the first private academy established in Pyŏngan Province, was founded in 1564, about twenty years after Paekundong sŏwŏn, the first private academy that unleashed the movement of founding private academies, was established by Chu Sebung in 1543 in Punggi, Kyŏngsang Province. A number of private academies and Confucian shrines were founded from the latter part of the sixteenth century on. Furthermore, there is evidence that Pyŏngan elites were operating smaller-scale private study halls from the sixteenth century on. As was the case in many academies and shrines built in other provinces in the following centuries, literati in Pyŏngan Province busied themselves with participating in this cultural movement of the time, as table 2 shows.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: It is true that, in the absolute number of private academies and shrines established during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, Pyŏngan Province lagged behind the southern provinces, and Kyŏngsang Province in particular. Even after the spread of Neo-Confucian studies, the depth of study in the region probably did not reach the level in the south, where philosophical debates and writings on Nature and Principle proliferated. Although the number of private academies increased, these schools did not provide the organizational or political support that northern scholars needed to advance in the central government. A few scholars were able to engage in debates with their southern contemporaries, but their scholarly accomplishments were modest and they failed to make political connections with any of the leading factions.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: Nonetheless, it remains arguable whether the low level of scholarship in Pyŏngan Province accounts for the political and social discrimination directed against the provinces people. Regional discrimination in the advancement of official careers was an integral part of a long process of marginalization of some members of the yangban ruling class—and of an accompanying concentration of central political power in the hands of a relatively small number of yangban groups residing in Seoul and its vicinity. In short, competition for power at the center continuously alienated scholar-officials from the central bureaucracy, beginning in the early Chosŏn dynasty. The first groups affected by this process were secondary sons of yangban and local power holders (hyangni 鄕吏) who were disqualified from the exams. Numerous literati purges and the subsequent development of hereditary factional strife from the sixteenth century on effectively severed the losers in these power games from access to central power. Cha Changsŏps study of political power groups in the late Chosŏn period epitomizes the political trend of consolidating power in a small circle of prominent families called pŏryŏl. The pŏryŏl were the capital-based families (kamun 家門) that produced officials who reached higher than senior third rank (tangsanggwan) for three generations successively. Cha identifies fifty-seven pŏryŏl that dominated political power and prestige since the reign of King Sŏnjo (r. 1567–1608) by manipulating civil service examinations, marriage ties with the royal family (as well as among themselves), protection privileges, and the institution of merit subject to maintain and perpetuate their privileged status (even though the strength of each family fluctuated over time).

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: In this game of narrowing down the power-sharing pool, northerners were easy prey because the far northern territory became a secure part of the Chosŏn state only in the latter part of the fifteenth century. To develop the area after incorporating it, the state forcefully relocated people to the north from the south, including criminals and corrupt administrators. The Confucian prejudice against any peripheral area that is physically distant from the center of civilization, and thus is regarded as crude and barbaric, may have provided an ideological justification for the political and social discrimination that the people from the northern region subsequently endured. Moreover, the political trend of sharing power among a limited group of yangban aristocracy at the center was well established by the seventeenth century. Given these facts, it is remarkable that northerners efforts at penetrating this exclusivity by emulating the dominant literati culture in the late Chosŏn succeeded in producing a relatively large number of munkwa degree-holders—and hardly surprising that their achievements did not extend to actually breaking down institutional discrimination and ushering in a meritocracy.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: Nevertheless, it is questionable whether Pyŏngan literati meant to admit any cultural inferiority when they referred to themselves as people of a remote area (hahyang or habang 遐鄉, 遐方), a term that reflects inferior social and intellectual status, as O Suchang argues. It seems that this expression was not used exclusively by Pyŏngan people and did not refer solely to Pyŏngan Province. In the Veritable Records of the Chosŏn Dynasty, it often indicates any geographically remote region, including the Yŏngnam area. Paek repeatedly emphasizes that it was out of modesty and a form of self-criticism that Pyŏngan literati admitted their scholarly achievements to be inadequate. As Paek indicates, political discrimination and social contempt were so deeply entrenched that the Pyŏngan people reached the point of self-abandonment. This may have forced them to use such self-degrading terminology, internalizing the prevailing literati discourse of the time.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: Paek argues that these three points are only excuses, and advocates reform of discriminatory practices against northerners in terms of official advancement on the part of the central court. He criticizes the courts rigid attitude, which held that the practice of prohibiting Pyŏngan residents from obtaining prestigious positions (chisaek 枳寨)” could not be altered because it was a long-held tradition. Indeed, Paek asserts, the court held on to this idea as though it had inherited some great principle that Heaven had bestowed and Earth embraced. Resorting to a Confucian dictum, he appeals to high officials at the court, saying:

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: Not changing [things] for three years is the great rule of the human Way. Yet Confucian scholars of the past still said, Why should one wait for three years if that were not the Way? Now, is blocking [people from Pyŏngan Province from prestigious positions] the unchangeable law of the dynasty? Or is it an instruction of great sages and canons? It is nothing but mistaken discussion by civil officials that cannot even be verified. What kind of Way and Principle is it to still pick it up and tenaciously hold on to it? Suppose that sŏin indeed committed crimes that deserve to bring about the prohibition. Rewards reach down for five generations, whereas punishment does not impact the son of the criminal. Thus, two hundred years [of prohibition] would be regarded as too long a time. Therefore, as for present-day discrimination, how can it not be resented? It is really so.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: Before Paek makes his final appeal, he goes over the efforts that previous kings had made to abolish such discriminatory practices. At the same time, he resents the fact that no kings words have had any effect in rectifying the situation because each monarchs subjects have been unwilling to carry out his orders. Paek concludes by urging the State Council to take his words seriously, discuss the matter at court, and follow the great benevolence of previous kings to clear away several hundred years of injustice, so that people from Pyŏngan Province can be treated the same way as people of other provinces.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: Indeed, Chosŏn kings had received numerous written and oral appeals about this issue, submitted by northerners and non-northerners alike. Subscribing to the Confucian notion that recruiting talented people was the most critical requirement of good government, they demanded that the practice of hereditary preference be mended. Korean kings wholeheartedly agreed with the memorialists and issued orders to employ and promote people according to their ability and talent. Obviously, these orders fell on deaf ears, as Paek lamented, and were never fully realized until the late nineteenth century.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: TRIALS AND CHOICESPaeks bitter criticism of discriminatory politics did not prevent him from pursuing his official career; rather, he seems to have sought ways to recover his opportunity to earn a position at the central court. For one thing, Paek paid great attention to the gravesites of his deceased ancestors, for he, like many other people at the time, believed in geomantic blessings supposedly emanating from auspicious gravesites. He relied on professional geomancers in selecting auspicious sites, though his teacher Hwagok, who was proficient in geomancy, also made authoritative contributions. Yet reliance on geomantic benefit alone would not have brought practical consequences. In concert with looking for geomantic gain, Paek sought favors from high, powerful officials at the court by paying visits to them. For example, he traveled to Seoul late in the fourth lunar month of 1801, and stayed there for four months, until he finally received an appointment as Fourth Secretary at the Bureau of Royal Rituals (Pongsangsi Chŏmjŏng 奉常寺僉正, Sr.4) with the assistance of Yi Ingmo, one of the ministers at the time. In a section of his collected works entitled Career History (hwanhae chingbi 宦海懲毖), Paek recorded the names of certain officials (who probably supported his attainment of such appointments) immediately after the entry for each new position he held after 1801.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: The most critical moment in Paeks political life occurred in 1812, when the Hong Kyŏngnae Rebellion broke out in his home region with strong support from the local elite. Both his regional identity and his loyalty to the ruling dynasty were tested. A few months before the rebellion, in his position as the Inspector of Pyŏngan Province (Tosa 都事, Jr.5), Paek had advised Provincial Governor Yi Mansu on the situation in the province, at Yis request. Paek pointed out that the commoners of the province were distressed over corruption and heavy taxation while the elite greatly resented the political discrimination they faced. On top of that, people had suffered severely that year from an unprecedentedly poor harvest. Bands of thieves had caused much trouble in Sangwŏn and Kwaksan, Pyŏngan Province. Under such circumstances, he foretold, there would be a revolt if relief measures were not taken immediately. In particular, Paek emphasized that the court should make every effort to search for talented men in the region and employ them. Because Paek correctly predicted social disturbances, Yi suspected him of involvement in the rebellion and denied him access to Pyŏngyang when he arrived there—several days, in fact, after rebellion had broken out on the eighteenth day of the twelfth lunar month of 1811.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: There are suspicious aspects to Paeks attitude and whereabouts during the rebellion. According to his diary, he happened to be at the district office of Chŏngju the day after the rebels had occupied two nearby districts, Kasan and Kwaksan. While he was there, the rebels, led by Choe Iryun, a local yangban of Chŏngju, broke into the jail to free a compatriot. Noticing that the magistrate of Chŏngju, Yi Yŏngsik, was unable to control the terrifying situation, Paek tried to persuade Kim Idae, the director of the local yangban bureau (Chwasu 座首), to suppress the rebels and defend the district by beheading Choe and his followers, not knowing that Kim himself had already joined the rebellion. Unsuccessful in convincing Kim, Paek returned home and began to gather like-minded people to counterattack the rebels. In his diary, he wrote that he spent several days amid chaos (even his aunt died on the twentieth). He left for Pyŏngyang on the evening of the twenty-third, five days after the rebellion began, and arrived there on the twenty-sixth.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: Like many other parts of Paeks diary, the entries about the 1812 Rebellion must have been written after the fact, when he had had a chance to review the situation. From both this diary and other historical records, there is no clear evidence proving that Paek committed himself to the rebel cause in the beginning and changed his position later on. Nonetheless, several points are suspect. First, he justified his loyalist position by emphasizing that he had tried to persuade Kim Idae to turn back the clock and suppress the rebels. But it is equally possible that Kim for his own part tried to gain Paeks approval and cooperation. Kims social standing was comparable to Paeks; he was a lower civil service exam degree holder (chinsa 進士). The Yŏnan Kim lineage, to which Kim belonged, was the most successful lineage in Chŏngju in producing munkwa passers, and had maintained many marriage ties with Paeks lineage. Some of Kims fellow yangban in the area had already committed themselves to the rebels at the preparation stage, and the rebels continuously strove to enlist the powerful local yangban in support of their cause. Moreover, the rebels manifesto stressed that the primary reason they revolted was their discontent over regional discrimination. As is evident in his writings, Paek shared resentment over unfair political practices with other members of the regional elite, so he may well have sympathized with the rebel leaders feelings.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: Second, two of the top leaders of the rebellion, Hong Kyŏngnae and U Kunchik, were geomancers—the theory of dynastic change based on geomancy played an important role in gathering support for the rebels—and Paek believed in geomancy. Third, it is puzzling that Paek managed to leave the Chŏngju district walled town when it was already in rebel hands if he adamantly opposed the rebels. Fourth, his explanation for his delay in returning to his post in Pyŏngyang is unsatisfactory. Thus it is not unreasonable to suppose that Paek may have considered participating in the rebel leadership. At the very least, he and his colleagues probably closely monitored the progress of the rebels activities before reaching a firm decision not to side with them.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: Such opportunistic thinking was so endemic that any substantial effort by volunteer leaders from Pyŏngan Province to counterattack the rebels emerged only after the rebel force had shown signs of division and weakness. Above all, the rebels did not provide organizational and ideological measures sufficient to solve the problems at hand in collective action, such as those associated with public goods and free riders. To certain groups of local elite—particularly munkwa passers and their families, who occupied the highest circle in the local hierarchy—the possibility of achieving the ultimate goal of dynastic change, as set forth by the rebellion, probably looked slim, while the risks far outweighed the promised political gain at the end of prolonged struggle. And although they shared the rebels concern over regional discrimination, the fact that they had been receiving benefits from the existing leadership made their political position a defensive and conservative one.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: In Paeks case, his cultural identity as a learned scholar-official pledging loyalty to the reigning royal house must have had more influence on his decision than his regional identity and admittedly sharp discontent. Neo-Confucian ideology, with its rigid demands of loyalty and righteousness, had long been a critical instrument in drawing even the disgruntled elite into the system and in suppressing their desire to revolt. Despite his resentment over the unjust political culture at the central court, Paek did not neglect to reiterate that he owed his well-being to his kings favor. Indeed, he never blamed any king for perpetuating regional discrimination. The targets of his criticism were, rather, the central yangban ministers who stubbornly discriminated against Pyŏngan residents and who objected to any rectification of this unreasonable practice. In addition, elite opportunism cannot be ignored as a contributing factor. Historically, those who sided with the royal cause during times of internal as well as external disturbances received huge material rewards and official ranks and titles that greatly boosted their social and political positions. This legalist prescription of reward and punishment must have been firmly integrated in the thinking of yangban elites and hence dictated their decisions.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: Paek Kyŏnghaes family had established itself as a renowned yangban family by the late eighteenth century, but it was because of the loyal death during the 1812 Rebellion of Paek Kyŏnghan, Kyŏnghaes older brother, that the family earned the courts attention and began to enjoy substantial prestige. The fact that seven of Paeks fathers descendants passed the munkwa between 1831 and 1885 indicates this growing favor. On a personal level, Paeks own career began to shine, and he broke through another difficult barrier in court hierarchy and qualified for one of the prestigious positions (chŏngjik) in 1816, when he was appointed Third Inspector of the Office of the Inspector-General (Sahŏnbu Changnyŏng 司憲府掌令, Sr.4). This was a moment of great honor for a man from Pyŏngan Province. Throughout Paeks diary, only a small number of people from Pyŏngan are recorded as passing this bureaucratic barrier: Paek Inhwan in 1787, Yi Ŭnggo in 1799, Kim Chosŏp in 1816, Paeks nephew, Yi Kijun, in 1830, and Paeks second son, Paek Chŏnggŏl, in 1835. Paek tackled the final hurdle on the bureaucratic ladder when he received the honorary ministerial rank (tangsanggwan) of Tongjŏng taebu (通政大夫, Sr.3) at the age of sixty-three, as a reward for his involvement in the revision of the royal genealogy. Finally, he obtained a tangsanggwan rank of Kasŏn taebu (嘉善大夫, Jr.2) at the age of seventy-two, and a junior second-rank position of Second Magistrate of the Seoul Magistracy when he was seventy-five years old.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: COMPROMISEThe violent way in which the rebels sought to break down regional discrimination failed and brought little change to the exclusionary political culture of the nineteenth-century Chosŏn court. An episode in 1818, at the height of Paeks official career, provides a vivid picture of the discriminatory treatment that the men of Pyŏngan Province suffered and of their responses to it, along with an understanding of the position of Paek himself, who was by then a venerated senior official from the region. The incident began with an altercation between Yi Hyŏngju, a Historian (Kyŏmsa) from Chŏngju, and Kwŏn Tonin, another Historian (Hallim 翰林) of lesser rank from the capital region, over whether to prohibit all those with the rank of Kyŏmsa from smoking inside the residential hall where they stayed when at court.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: To understand this incident, an explanation of the delicate court hierarchical order, which did not precisely correlate with the ranking system, is needed. The Kyŏmsa was a historian position held by mid- to low-ranking officials concurrently with other offices, such as positions in the Office of Royal Decrees (Yemungwan), the Royal Secretariat (Sŭngjŏngwŏn), the Office of the Censor-General (Saganwŏn), and the six ministries. It was presumably a prestigious position (chŏngyojik), both because its holders worked physically very close to the king and because what they recorded became the main sources of dynastic history. Despite a working environment that provided frequent contact with high-ranking officials as well as with the king himself, Kyŏmsa from Pyŏngan Province were unable to obtain a status equal to that of historians from other regions. Rather, as previously mentioned, they were subject to jibes such as one that claimed the Kyŏmsa position to be not much different from that of a eunuch. They simply depended on the favor of the king, who supposedly held the ultimate power to promote and demote his officials. The contempt they received from high-ranking officials, however, became progressively worse, and even young capital aristocrats who held prestigious offices (chŏngyojik) at court emulated the practice of heaping scorn on Kyŏmsa from Pyŏngan Province.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: The incident of 1818 involved two different types of historian positions—Kyŏmsa and Yemungwan Hallim, which was a lower rank than Kyŏmsa but a chŏngyojik envied by successful munkwa candidates. Apparently, people from Pyŏngan Province were in practice not assigned to this office. On the seventeenth day of the sixth lunar month of 1818, Hallim Kwŏn Tonin insulted Kyŏmsa Yi Hyŏngju by insisting that he refrain from smoking in the residential hall so as not to confuse the distinction between men from Pyŏngan and other areas. Enraged by this direct insult, Yi left the office after some quarreling. This incident incited all the court officials from Pyŏngan Province, who discussed the possibility of resigning as a group. Paek objected to this idea, reminding them that the position of the Kwansŏ region (Pyŏngan Province) had become much more perilous ever since the 1812 rebellion. Thus he advised them to be cautious. Despite Paeks advice, all three Kyŏmsa from Pyŏngan Province decided to resign.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: The next day, Assistant Section Chief of the Ministry of War Kim Chitae (Pyŏngjo Chwarang) from Kaesŏng, Hwanghae Province, attempted to make peace between the Hallim and Kyŏmsa, but this only fanned the flames of the confrontation. Kwŏn Tonin abruptly made a rash comment that a rebellion like that of Hong Kyŏngnae would soon break out. At the time, not all the court officials from Pyŏngan Province were united. Kim Ijŏk from Kangdong attended the court and thus betrayed their resolution to resign as a group. He even sided with Kwŏn by tattling on Kim Chigu, who had threatened to break his leg if he attended the court again the next day. Due to their boycott, the Royal Secretariat demanded that the three Kyŏmsa be arrested and investigated. Soon after, three other senior northerners, including Paek himself, were accused of coaxing the Kyŏmsa and leading people from Pyŏngan Province to resign their positions. After several days of investigation and flogging, Paek and the others were sentenced to exile. However, recognizing Paeks brother Kyŏnghans loyal death at the time of 1812 rebellion, Paek was forgiven, along with the others implicated in the incident. In his diary, Paek deplores the incident, noting that Kyŏmsa is a historian; so is Hallim. In the court structure, Hallim holds a chamoe 參外 position while Kyŏmsa holds that of chamsang. The discussion of making a distinction between this and that is nonsense. Despite his resentment, Paeks position at the time of the 1818 episode was very conservative and prudent, as a person who had already been designated a loyal subject and who had been heavily rewarded.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: CONCLUSIONPaek Kyŏnghaes lifetime roughly coincided with the culmination of “practices of exclusion,” whereby members of the central aristocratic elite protected their status and privileges. Regional discrimination was an integral part of such long-term practices that marginalized various status groups during the Chosŏn dynasty. This trend had begun as early as the founding of the dynasty, when regulations had restricted local power holders (hyangni) from sitting for the civil service examinations. Such discriminatory acts were soon critically applied to the secondary sons of yangban. Furthermore, the competition for power at the center continuously alienated yangban elites from the central bureaucracy from the early Chosŏn period on, which marginalized the yangban ruling class and concentrated central political power around a few capital-based yangban groups.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: These practices of exclusion and monopoly of power by a few central yangban contradict a fundamental Neo-Confucian prescription of meritocracy, according to which the monarch rules the country by recruiting men of talent, not men with privileged family backgrounds. Those who were excluded, but advocated meritocracy, challenged these aspects of political culture that deviated from Confucian norms. Both practitioners of exclusion and those who were excluded shared the culture of Neo-Confucian values, beliefs, and rituals. Thus it was not a matter of the voices calling for abolition of unfair and unethical employment practices never reaching sympathetic ears. Rather, it took an enormous amount of effort and time to carry out any legal reform that might possibly curtail the privileges of the central power group. And, to the profound disappointment to the victims of discrimination, legal changes never seemed to be implemented.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: Paeks experiences as a scholar-official and his responses to the various crises he faced during his tumultuous official career epitomize the ordeals that a talented man lacking a proper pedigree had to undergo within the inflexible Chosŏn sociopolitical system, which deviated from ideal Confucian prescriptions and precepts. The processes required to gain entry into the nexus of the privileged were exasperating and necessitated continuous negotiation of various sets of identities. Throughout his life, Paek ardently supported undoing the wrongs dealt out to him and his colleagues from Pyŏngan Province, though not to the extent that he risked his own privileged status or betrayed his Confucian standards. When Paek was finally forced to choose between the existing dynastic system—which was obviously defective but which nevertheless granted him the honor of being a part of it (no matter how marginal a part)—and a group of his fellow men who were resolved to rid themselves of regional discrimination through violence, his loyalist decision was predictable (albeit neither easy nor spontaneous), and undeniably rewarding in the long run.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: Paeks writings paint an ambivalent picture at first glance. They are full of anger, frustration, and accusations over the issue of regional discrimination. At the same time, they reveal that Paek was thoroughly indoctrinated into Neo-Confucian state ideology, in which the monarchical system and individual loyalty to it were idealized and demanded. Paek vehemently resented the discriminatory political culture that disadvantaged him and his colleagues from Pyŏngan Province. Nonetheless, he blamed such practices not on the royal house but on the narrow-minded central aristocracy that unfairly perpetuated such ill-conceived practices. Thus he found no ideological justification for taking part in a rebellious and aggressive movement against the crown to rectify the grievances that Pyŏngan people, including himself, suffered.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Negotiating Cultural Identities in Conflict - A Reading of the Writings of Paek Kyonghae 1765-1842
essay_text: In addition, no matter how much discrimination Paek personally faced from central aristocrats, he remained a participant in the central political process (however marginally) and earned fame as one of very few renowned scholar-officials from the northwestern region. The reputation and culture that Paek and his family enjoyed must have contributed to molding his conservative position of preserving the existing Chosŏn ideology and institutions. Because he did not envision any swift structural change, his solution to the problem of regional discrimination was passive and individualistic. Nevertheless, his advocacy for his home province—together with succeeding efforts launched by the next generation of Pyŏngan literati—eventually, if slowly, came to fruition. Paeks second son, Chŏnggŏl, passed the munkwa in 1831 and was unprecedentedly assigned to the Office of Diplomatic Correspondence. Of such an incredible moment, Paek wrote, This is the first such occasion in some hundred years in the history of Pyŏngan Province. I am delighted on the one hand; I feel anxious on the other hand.

author: John Duncan
essay_title: Origins of the Choson Dynasty - Intro Conclusion
essay_text: In the seventh month of 1392 the 474-year-old Koryŏ dynasty came to an end, its place as ruler of the Korean Peninsula taken by a new dynasty, the Chosŏn. Dynastic changes were rare, this being the only one in the thousand years preceding Japanese colonization in 1910. It has, as a consequence, attracted a great deal of scholarly attention.

author: John Duncan
essay_title: Origins of the Choson Dynasty - Intro Conclusion
essay_text: The Koryŏ did not meet its doom at the hands of foreign invaders, as did the Sung (960–1279) and the Ming (1368–1644) in China. Neither did it fall to provincially based rebel movements, as did China’s Han (206 BCE–CE 220) and Yüan (1279–1368) dynasties or Korea’s Silla (?–935). The dynasty, which survived serious revolts in the early twelfth century, a military coup in 1170, conquest by the Mongols in the mid-thirteenth century, and the deposal and assassination of many of its kings throughout its five centuries, was in the end done in by its own officials.

author: John Duncan
essay_title: Origins of the Choson Dynasty - Intro Conclusion
essay_text: A variety of assessments of this event has been advanced within larger schemes of historical interpretation. Traditional Confucian views emphasized the moral depravity of the final Koryŏ kings and the ethical virtues of Yi Sŏng-gye, the founding monarch of the new dynasty. In the early twentieth century historian-apologists for imperial Japan argued, as part of an effort to depict Korea as a backward and historically stagnant society in need of enlightened (Japanese) leadership, that the Koryŏ-Chosŏn change of dynasties was a mere palace coup of no real historical significance. The main thrust of the imperialist view was that Korea had not followed the proper ancient-medieval-modern path of historical development that had supposedly been taken by the “advanced countries” (J. senjinkoku, K. sŏnjin’guk) of Western Europe and, of course, Japan. Various aspects of Korea’s past were depicted in negative terms: political subservience to China and lack of autonomy; socioeconomic stagnancy and omission of the feudal stage of development; and cultural imitation of China and lack of creativity. In short, the Japanese applied to Korea the same notion of an unchanging traditional order that Western imperialist powers used against non-Western, “pre-modern” societies.

author: John Duncan
essay_title: Origins of the Choson Dynasty - Intro Conclusion
essay_text: Korean scholars struggled to rebut the imperialist view throughout the colonial period. Men such as Sin Ch’ae-ho, Pak Ŭn-sik, and Chŏng In-bo, referred to as “nationalist historians” (minjokchuŭi sahakcha,) sought to define the Korean nation in terms of a unique spirit, the recovery of which would enable Koreans to free themselves of the shackles of foreign domination and to revitalize their country. Another group, known as “positivist historians” (silchŭng sahakcha,) included men such as Yi Hong-jik and Yi Pyŏng-do who were trained at Japanese universities and strove to counter imperialist depictions of Korean history, particularly the ancient period, through rigorous use of documentary evidence. A third group, usually called “socioeconomic historians” (sahoe kyŏngje sahakcha), was influenced by leftist ideas. In their efforts to refute Japanese contentions of stagnation, men such as Paek Nam-un and Yi Ch’ŏng-wŏn eschewed Marx’s idea of an Asiatic mode of production and applied instead a Stalinist interpretation, claiming that Korea, too, had passed through ancient slave and medieval feudal stages of development. Although these colonial era scholars labored under great political difficulties, their work laid down the foundations of modern Korean historiography and, in terms of basic approaches, still provides points of departure for scholarship in the late twentieth century.

author: John Duncan
essay_title: Origins of the Choson Dynasty - Intro Conclusion
essay_text: These early efforts not withstanding, it was not until after Japan withdrew in 1945 that Koreans were free to engage in the study of their past. Historical scholarship since 1945 has devoted much energy to refuting the stagnation theory. North Korean scholars have generally followed the lead of Paek Namun in applying a Stalinist model of historical analysis that seeks to fit the Korean past into slave, feudal, and capitalist stages of historical development. Their interpretation, however, does not assign great significance to the founding of the Chosŏn dynasty because they see it as essentially a reconsolidation of feudal institutions within a lengthy medieval period that began with the rise of the Three Kingdoms (Silla; Paekche, ?–660; Koguryŏ, ?–668) nearly two thousand years ago and ended in the nineteenth century.

author: John Duncan
essay_title: Origins of the Choson Dynasty - Intro Conclusion
essay_text: South Korean historical scholarship has been more diverse. The immediate post-1945 period saw a perpetuation of all three main colonial era approaches. There were the “new nationalists” (sin minjokchuŭija), such as Son Chin-t’ae, who contended that the Korean nation (minjok) had been formed in prehistoric times and who sought to define the nation in terms of its unique cultural and spiritual aspects, arguing that the singularity of the Korean historical experience meant that it could not and should not be forced into either Western European or Marxist models. A number of socioeconomic historians, such as Chŏn Sŏk-tam, continued the effort to fit Korean history into a Stalinist model. Positivist historians such as Yi Pyŏng-do and Yi Sang-baek, who were ensconced in history departments at major universities at the time of liberation, criticized both the nationalist and the socioeconomic historians for their excessive devotion to abstract theory. As a result of the Korean War and the postwar political climate, positivist historians came to dominate the field in South Korea during the 1950s and 1960s.

author: John Duncan
essay_title: Origins of the Choson Dynasty - Intro Conclusion
essay_text: By the mid-1960s positivists came under increasing criticism for their excessive devotion to digging out facts without providing a conceptual framework for interpretation. By the end of the decade there was a growing tendency, informed—perhaps unwittingly in some cases—by Stalinist analytical categories, to view Korea’s history as a process of developmental stages propelled by the rise to power of successive new socioeconomic classes, although the South Korean scholars usually avoided the term “class” (kyegŭp) in favor of politically less sensitive terms such as “ruling stratum” (chibae ch’ŭng). Cognizant of the difficulties inherent in trying to force Korea’s history into the three-stage model, these scholars applied a modified periodization to Korean history that focused on such events as the Silla-Koryŏ transition, the mid-Koryŏ ascendancy of great central official descent groups, the military coup of 1170, the rise of the rusticated literati (sarim) in the sixteenth century, and the advent of reform Confucianism, commonly known as Practical Learning (Sirhak), in the late Chosŏn and argued that these phenomena reflected the rise of new socioeconomic forces.

author: John Duncan
essay_title: Origins of the Choson Dynasty - Intro Conclusion
essay_text: This approach, known as the “internal development theory” (naejaejŏk palchŏn non), was given its classic formulation in Lee Ki-baik’s influential book Han’guksa sillon (translated into English as A New History of Korea). I can still remember the keen sense of excitement I felt when I read Professor Lee’s book for the first time as an undergraduate. Here, at last, I believed, was a way to reconcile the unique aspects of Korean history with universalistic models.

author: John Duncan
essay_title: Origins of the Choson Dynasty - Intro Conclusion
essay_text: As I proceeded in my graduate studies, however, I became increasingly skeptical of the internal development theory. In part, I was influenced by the new “people’s history” (minjung sahak) of the 1980s, which, while clinging to the notion of Korean history as a process of linear development, criticized mainstream historians because their emphasis on ruling classes, rather than the people, as the prime movers of history legitimated the capitalist establishment in contemporary South Korea and provided an ideological prop for the developmentalist state of Park Chung Hee and Chun Doo Hwan.
