Economic disparities must have existed between the large landowning class and the poor cultivators, but various rural institutions led by the rural elite—such as village compacts (tongyak), kye-type financial cooperatives, labor-sharing arrangements, and lineage associations (munjung) that controlled lineage assets and rituals—played an important role in redistributing resources. In particular, the rural elite not only directly oversaw all the activities of the cultivators but also maintained close ties with them because they, unlike Japanese and some Chinese absentee landlords, did live in the countryside with other economically less fortunate residents. A moral economy that guaranteed minimal subsistence through shared moral values and communal institutions may also have mitigated the escalation of class tension. Rural populations of various economic resources and social backgrounds in villages were intricately connected to one another and heavily interdependent in managing their livelihoods; thus, their political behaviors were also affected by these lines of networks rather than by class interests alone.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: TAXESThe problem that caused the most discord between the district government and the people in Chinju in 1862 was the governments effort to make up for the lost principal of the grain loan reserve by levying arbitrary taxation on land. The original purpose of establishing the grain loan system (hwan’gok) at the beginning of the Chosŏn dynasty had been to provide relief to people at the time of the spring grain shortage. In the beginning, grain loans were distributed to the people interest free; later, in order to make up for incidental losses in handling and storage, a 2 percent interest rate was charged on these loans. Because relief and other reserves could not be replenished by such means, interest rates were raised after the mid-fifteenth century; they were set at 10 percent by the end of fifteenth century, even though it was already clear that the people were incapable of repaying the principal, let alone the interest. Additional changes took place when the government began to use interest as part of state revenues by requiring that one-tenth of the interest to be sent to the Ministry of Taxation as a recording fee. Other government agencies then began to use grain loans to meet their expenses, and this practice expanded over time. By the eighteenth century, almost every government office, whether in the provinces or in the capital, was loaning out its grain reserves with interest in order to raise funds.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: When the whole grain loan system was transformed into a kind of taxation—and local administrators were put in charge of managing the loans without strict regulations to follow or close supervision over the system—numerous problems emerged. First of all, given the high rate of default on debts, the only way to meet revenue and reserve requirements was to manipulate the grain stocks, falsify the granary ledgers, and extort grain from borrowers. The arbitrary and forced distribution of loans to people who did not need them (in order to obtain interest payments) became widespread. Magistrates often targeted rich households to ensure the collection of revenue. At times, wealthy households were forced to receive a share of grain, often on paper only, and to pay the interest (hŏrok). Even though this transfer of financial burden to the wealthy can be seen as a move toward a more egalitarian distribution of wealth—and as a progressive taxing structure that broke the traditional attachment of social status to the taxing mechanism—the arbitrary collection of interest from wealthy but powerless households in the countryside became a critical element in their resentment against the district government and, subsequently, against the state itself, which did not heed their complaints.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: In addition, local administrators took advantage of territorial price variations to profit by shifting grain reserves from areas of glut to areas of shortage (imu). They sold off the grain at high prices and restocked it at low prices, appropriating the difference. The manipulation of measures at the time of distribution and repayment was also a widespread method that administrators used to make a profit. Last but not least, they cashed in on loan transactions by controlling cash-grain conversion rates. Tax administrators used these methods not solely to line their own pockets but also as a viable way of maintaining the grain reserves, which would otherwise have decreased over time because of the basic penury of the rural population. The problem was that the market did not always work in their favor. In other words, territorial price variations and cash-grain conversion rates could be adversely affected by price fluctuations following both good harvests and bad ones. The final result of the borrowers inability to repay their debts (minpo), incidental losses attributable to mismanagement of funds, and official and unofficial embezzlement by clerks (ipo) and magistrates was the substantial loss of principal. To make up for the loss of grain loans evidently caused by embezzlement, local administrators added surtaxes on land and households. This arbitrary and sudden tax increase was one of the direct causes of the popular riots in 1862.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: The violent explosion of popular resentment occurred only after protracted efforts to rectify the wrongs in the tax system by following the legal prescriptions for doing so. The people of Chinju lodged their complaints about the problems related to grain loans as early as 1849, when Pak Suik and others appealed directly to the king by blocking his procession and striking a gong to attract royal attention (kyŏkchaeng). They protested that people could not bear the added burden caused by dramatic increases in the grain loan reserves from 50,000 sŏm to 150,000 sŏm over the previous ten years (Ilsŏngnok, 1849/11/19; Song Ch’ansŏp 2003, 17). Apparently, additional charges had been collected from the land (kyŏlching or kyŏllyŏm) since 1855 in order to make up for the loss of grain reserves. Two yang of cash per kyŏl were levied every once in a while, which amounted to more than 180,000 yang between 1855 and 1859. This tax was suspended in 1859 when a group from Chinju traveled to Hansŏng (Seoul), the capital, and appealed to the Border Defense Command (Pibyŏnsa) for its abolition (Ilsŏngnok, 1859/6/19; Song Ch’ansŏp 2003, 17–18). In 1861, the magistrate Sin Ok tried to levy 2 yang, 5 chŏn per kyŏl to refill the loss of grain reserves, but he had to yield because the people again prepared to appeal to the Border Defense Command (CCCT, 179–80; Yi Myŏngyun 1862, 22-30).

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: Upon taking office as magistrate in 1861, Hong Pyŏngwŏn examined the financial condition of Chinju District and found that 28,649 sŏm out of 47,386 sŏm from the grain loan reserves had disappeared and that there was no way to refill them (Pibyŏnsa tŭngnok, 1861/11/26; 1862 nyŏn nongmin hangjaeng, 133). According to the investigation launched by Special Commissioner (Anhaeksa) Pak Kyusu (1807–77) after the rebellion, out of total grain reserves in excess of 50,000 sŏm, more than 40,000 sŏm had been lost, mostly because of embezzlement and mismanagement of funds by previous magistrates, local clerks (hyangni or ajŏn), and capital liaison clerks (kyŏngjŏri) over the years (Imsullok, 9–10). The capital and provincial liaison masters (kyŏngjuin and yŏngjuin) made choch’ae, a kind of public loan, to local clerks, boatmen, and others at relatively high interest rates by using as principal the tax revenues under their care. Problems arose when the debtors were unable to repay what they had borrowed from the liaison masters. For example, Yang Chaesu, an earlier capital liaison master, had loaned out money to boatmen in charge of transporting tax grain to the capital so that they could meet their expenses for the job. When the debtors could not repay the loan, Yang appropriated a public fund of 24,000 yang, from which he personally took 14,000 yang as payment of the loans that he could not collect from the borrowers. The remaining 10,000 yang were loaned out to other people with interest for thirteen years, which would have ultimately made up for the loss in the total. Other earlier capital liaison masters copied Yangs practice and collected unpaid personal loans from public funds, listing borrowers names on the grain loan roster as though they were loaning them funds from the grain reserves. These debtors had no way of paying back these amounts, which were ultimately transferred to the ordinary people as surcharges on land (Imsullok, 10).

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: Chŏng Yagyong (1762–1836), a late Chosŏn scholar, criticized the harm done by local clerks, noting that the people rely on land for their livelihood, whereas local clerks regard the people as their land” (1818, 2:291). It is true that local administrators were corrupt and that they became the primary targets of the popular riots of 1862. Yet the institutional and structural arrangements that were conducive to their corrupt behavior must also be considered. First of all, local clerks were the ones who provided basic services and expertise to the magistrate, who was usually a stranger to local conditions. Because they were not officially compensated, however, they had to rely on fees and surcharges in return for their services. They were able to do this because the tax structure was very elastic, so that tax items could be created under various pretexts. In addition, because each item was levied on different taxable sources, such as land and households, the complete tax administrative structure was very confusing and complicated. As a corollary, local administrators could easily manipulate the distribution and collection of taxes; people paid taxes without knowing why they had to pay such an amount (Chŏng Yagyong 1817, 7: 7b-8a). In a word, random taxation was institutionally guaranteed, and almost all strata of the rural population suffered official corruption derived from structural defects in the local government.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: The pressure on the magistrates, who were responsible for the sound maintenance of local finances, was great. In 1862, Chinju magistrate Hong Pyŏngwŏn called for meetings of local yangban and instructors (Hunjang) from each subdistrict to obtain their cooperation in imposing the consolidated land tax (togyŏl), for it was the most convenient and secure means of replenishing reserves for local administrators at the time. Hong set the rate (kyŏlka) drastically high, at 6 yang, 5 chŏn (CCCT, 180). There must have been certain divisions of opinion among members of the local elite. For example, former fifth counselor at the Office of the Special Counselors (Hongmungwan Kyori) Yi Myŏngyun (1804–63), a member of the Chŏnju Yi descent group, did not approve the decision and led the early protest movements in Chinju. To make matters worse, Hong Pyŏngwŏns decision was soon followed by that of Military Commander Paek Naksin, who coerced the local elite (tumin) into approving an extra levy on households (tonghwan) to make up for the lost funds. The Military Commanders Office of Right Kyŏngsang Province, which had its own grain reserve quota and earned revenue by loaning out its reserves, had lost almost 24,154 sŏm over the years from its total quota of 39,218 sŏm, attributable primarily to embezzlement by clerks (Imsullok, 8, 12; CCCT, 189–90).

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: The consolidated land tax began to be used in some local districts in the early nineteenth century and soon spread to most other districts in the southern provinces. With the adoption of the consolidated land tax, not only were all taxes (including a portion of the military tax and grain loan interest) fused into a single land levy, but also they were collected in cash under the direct supervision of the magistrate. Prior to this, tax collection had been the responsibility of a head household (hosu), which was the representative of a certain number of households whose total land possessions amounted to 8 kyŏl. The new method of direct tax collection sought to avoid the services of intermediaries, such as hosu and other quasi-administrative officials at the subdistrict levels (myŏnim and iim), for the collection and transportation of taxes. At the outset, people regarded direct tax collection as a good system because the fees and surcharges saved in the process of collecting and delivering taxes to the designated central or provincial offices were used to make up for shortages in other taxation, such as the military tax and miscellaneous local government expenses. This new direct taxation thus could have alleviated previous inequities stemming from exemption privileges for the yangban and the rich, in that the tax obligation was, in principle, to be spread evenly over all households on the basis of land ownership, irrespective of social status.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: The consolidated land tax was a spontaneous response to the changing social and economic situation at the local level. First of all, it reflected the widespread use of currency by the nineteenth century. Overcoming popular distrust of the use of cash in the first half of the seventeenth century, which was a result of the rural economy remaining at the level of subsistence, cash had become a permanent feature of the Chosŏn economy ever since minting had been resumed in 1681 (Palais 1996, 853–76). Despite government conservatism in the use of cash, cash policy could not be rolled back (it also could not be rolled forward to adopt paper money or multiple-denomination cash) because of the gradual expansion of commercial economy since the seventeenth century. Along with the development of commercial activities, the government requirement that taxes be paid in cash became a primary motivation for people to use cash in the early stages of the cash economy. The percentage of cash in government revenues grew gradually, to the extent that in 1820, 52.8 percent of taxes were collected in cash, 29.2 percent in rice, and 14.1 percent in cotton and cotton cloth (Palais 1996, 998).

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: The new tax system was intended to lighten the tax burdens born by the rural populace, to spread them more equally, and to strengthen the local financial situation. However, problems in the management of the consolidated land tax not only created more critical damage to the rural economy but also aggravated the financial shortages of the local government because the system was operated on ad hoc basis without clear regulations set by the central government and thus left loopholes for manipulations. Rather than serving its intended purpose of providing relief to the people, the surplus earned by the manipulation of regional and temporal price differences and conversion rates came to be absorbed by local administrators. These administrators arbitrarily misappropriated this convenient taxing system on land and increased tax rates just to aggrandize private interests or to make up for losses created in other public funds, such as the grain loan system (which, as previously mentioned, was in arrears because of precisely such embezzlement and the borrowers inability to repay loans). The problems created in the operation of the consolidated land tax clearly reflected the general decay of the local tax administration and were most fiercely resented by the rebels in 1862.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: The causes of the popular uprising in Chinju were not just economic but political as well. When local clerks reaped profits by taking advantage of public loans and the market economy—transferring the losses caused by their unsuccessful commercial endeavors to taxpayers—the rural population, especially the rural elite, was enraged. Yet the source of their anger was not only the clerks unfair economic extraction but also the delicate shift in power relations that it implied. Clerks traditionally occupied intermediate ranks, at best, in the local administration. When they encroached on the carefully managed economic resources under the control of the rural elite, this redrew the lines of authority over local affairs. Moreover, the magistrate did nothing to prevent the power shift from taking place; on the contrary, he endorsed the situation. When the locus of power tipped toward the traditionally demeaned status group of local clerks—and toward the magistrate, who was an outsider—the local elite could not just stand by and watch.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: LEGAL APPROACHES

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: It is important here to consider who was most disadvantaged when the consolidated land tax was instituted. First it was intermediaries in the tax administration at the village and subdistrict levels, as they lost their jobs and fees. The social status of these quasi-officials is not clear, but they must have been people who had great interests or shares in tax distribution and collection and could exercise significant influence in village affairs. The possibility of commoners holding these positions cannot be excluded, though it is safe to assume that they were under the control of the local yangban, in light of social conditions during the late Chosŏn, when the yangban in general owned a great deal of land and exercised unyielding authority over local affairs.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: Second, landowners were affected. The yangban landowners particularly disliked the new system because it forced them to assume responsibility for a part of the military tax and grain loan interest from which they previously had been exempted but was now grafted onto ownership of land. As noted earlier, the main purpose of instituting the consolidated land tax was to make up for losses or shortages in taxation in most areas. This explains why some prominent yangban led the rebellions, demanding the abolition of the consolidated land tax or the reduction of the tax rate in a number of uprisings in 1862. Last but not least, the new system affected tenant farmers because landlords eventually transferred part or all of the extra taxation to tenants by increasing their rents.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: Reflecting the dynamic and complex social and economic conditions in the countryside, various social strata provided leadership for the popular uprisings in 1862. Nonetheless, it was the educated local elite who in many cases provided the initial leadership. Special Commissioner Pak Kyusu specifically indicated that it was the local yangban who were responsible for circulating letters, convening meetings, and provoking uprisings (Imsullok, 5, 23). In Chinju, the activities of Yi Myŏngyun from Ch’ukkok-ri are notable in the earlier stage of lodging complaints with the government. Although Yi denied leading the rebellion, it was understood that he had joined the conspiracy after his appeal to remove his estate from the consolidated land tax roster was rejected by the government (Imsullok, 32–33). Yi was probably furious, not just because he was being economically drained by the new system of taxation but also because his privileged status had been violated.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: Yis neighbor, Yu Kyech’un, was a poor yangban. He had been involved in submitting complaints and appeals about taxation to the government before 1862 and played the most visible role in the uprising by sending out circulars (t’ongmun), convening meetings, and composing vernacular songs to mobilize firewood-gatherers (ch’ogun). Yu, who reportedly owned no land, probably acted out of solidarity with his fellow yangban and not simply because of economic concerns (Imsullok, 24; Kim Chunhyŏng 2001, 58–59).

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: After the decision was made to institute the consolidated land tax at the local council meeting (hyanghoe) under the direction of magistrate Hong Pyŏngwŏn, Yi Myŏngyun and other yangban in the area met a few times to devise ways to challenge the decision. They gathered at the houses of fellow yangban Pak Suik and a private slave named Kŏmtong during the first lunar month of 1862 (Imsullok, 25, 32). They decided to have a districtwide meeting (tohoe or ŭphoe) at Sugok-ri on the sixth day of the second lunar month, which was a market day there, and sent out circulars to announce the meeting. Around this time, Yu Kyech’un composed a vernacular circular in the form of a song to recruit firewood-gatherers at the request of Yi Kyeyŏl, a second cousin of Yi Myŏngyun and the head of the firewood-gatherers association. At the Sugok meeting, more than three hundred influential personalities in the area discussed their greatest concerns. They agreed to send an appeal to the provincial governor in Taegu (ŭisong) requesting cancellation of the consolidated land tax, and they selected the representatives who would deliver it (CCCT, 180, 179).

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: ERUPTION OF VIOLENCENot everyone at the Sugok meeting supported the legal measure of submitting a written appeal to the provincial government. Yu Kyech’un, Sŏng Kyeju, and other local yangban elite insisted on the more aggressive strategies of sabotaging market day at the district seat, confronting the magistrate face to face, and destroying the houses of those who had supported the decision to institute the consolidated land tax. Although Yu was arrested by the Military Commanders Office immediately after the meeting as the ringleader of the assembly, further discussions on this line of action and recruitment of supporters seem to have taken place. On the fourteenth day of the second lunar month, a market day at Tŏksan-ri, people calling themselves firewood-gatherers” began their violent struggle by causing disturbances at the market and destroying the house of the instructor Yi Yunsŏ because he had joined the local council meeting convened by the magistrate and had supported the consolidated land tax. Tŏksan-ri was about 18 miles from the district seat, in the northwestern corner of Chinju District. From there, protestors swept through the western part of the district along the Tŏkch’ŏn River, rounding up supporters for a few days before arriving close to the district seat on the eighteenth day of the same month (CCCT, 180; Imsullok, 23–24).

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: The Chinju uprising has often been called “a rebellion by firewood-gatherers (chogun chakpyŏn) because firewood-gatherers played the most active role throughout the revolt. They were ordinary cultivators who also gathered firewood in the hills and mountains in the agricultural off-season. Because logs, branches, and dry leaves were the main source of heat and such resources were limited, competition had developed over the right to collect firewood in the countryside. By this time, strict rules by various community organizations, such as lineage associations and village compacts, had been devised to protect the limited resources and to control over competition among different interest groups. Firewood-gatherers had organized along lineage or village lines for the same purposes, most likely under the supervision of local elite. One clear example in relation to the Chinju rebellion is the firewood-gatherers organization headed by the aforementioned Yi Kyeyŏl, a close relative of Yi Myŏngyun and thus a yangban, though reportedly an uneducated one. He probably acted a proxy or liaison between the renowned yangban family headed by Yi Myŏngyun and the tenants and other people who were financially and socially related to the family. Using a vernacular manifesto composed by Yu Kyech’un, Yi Kyeyŏl mobilized the firewood-gatherers and participated in the Sugok meeting, as well as in protests at the district seat (Imsullok, 25, 32).

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: Thus, the participation of firewood-gatherers in the Chinju rebellion does not necessarily represent the explosion of accumulated class consciousness and class struggle against rural overlords. Special Commissioner Pak Kyusu accused the wealthy local elite who were most affected by the consolidated land tax and the extra levy on households of mobilizing ordinary rural residents to launch complaints and to force the magistrate to drop the additional taxes (Imsullok, 24; CCCT, 182). The fact that the mobilization for collective action often relied on local administrative or lineage organizations with the support of influential local elite does seem to support Paks observation. A yangban named Ho Ho, from Ch’ukkok-ri; a village administrator (tongim), Cho Sŏkch’ŏl; a subdistrict administrator (p’unghŏn), Hwang Ŭngsŏ; and a village head (tumin), Kim Chŏngsik, are all examples of local quasi-officials at the bottom of the administrative ladder who provided support in mobilizing people. Ha Ubŏm and Ha Hagun recruited their relatives for the rebellion; Pak Ch’ansun mobilized eight other relatives to join. Two slaves, Maengdol and Kwidae, led thirty other villagers to the rebel band (Imsullok, 26-29).

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: Therefore, it is difficult to believe that the participation of firewood-gatherers in the rebellion reflected class antagonism and nothing but class antagonism, in light of the presence of class differentiation found in the previously discussed analyses of landownership. According to Lucien Bianco (1986) in his study of popular rebellions in China, peasant material interests were invariably localistic, often cutting across class. Robert Marks, who views peasant revolutionary movements in southern China primarily as the product of class struggle, also recognizes that intervillage conflict over access to water and wood had a cross-class character. That is, class factors were marred by economic interests that were shared across village society as a whole (Marks 1984, 62–67).

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: These quasi-officials at the various levels of administrative units below the district level represented the crucial nexus of state-society contact. Although formal administrative, fiscal, military, and judicial powers were concentrated in the hands of the state-appointed magistrate, it was these locally selected dignitaries, whether yangban or commoners, who exercised substantial social and financial control over villagers lives. Crisscrossed with and overlapped by other types of village-level institutions, local affairs were managed by quasi-officials who therefore enjoyed considerable room to manipulate the power and authority delegated to them. Their orientation and motivation played a vital role in mobilizing popular participation in the 1862 rebellions, though their decision was not a unilateral one. In the course of the district governments tightening of local fiscal control (discussed earlier), some administrators saw opportunities to participate in the emerging taxation system on favored terms, whereas others grieved over what they felt was disadvantageous and unjust. It is impossible to know the individual circumstances under which subdistrict-level administrators took—or avoided taking—political action, though the importance of their agency in assuming leadership roles in the popular protest goes without saying.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: Kinship and communal activities, which provided a sense of solidarity among rural population, were great resources in mobilizing people for collective action. Yangban families in the countryside organized single-surname villages and lineage associations along the basis of bloodlines in an effort to protect financial resources, maintain social prestige, and control local population in the late Chosŏn. In addition to blood ties, villages must have shared some economic interests in maintaining water control, the most important resource for farming. Also, it was typical for a landowner to have small parcels of land in many different villages, which tended to promote cross-village unity. The same could be said of tenants who rented land that was located beyond their own villages. Thus, people of different villages had some contact with one another and shared similar concerns. As seen in Chinju and most other districts, villages often joined the uprisings as a whole. The quota system in the management of taxation, which required collective responsibility in tax payment and had been devised for administrative convenience on the part of the local government, brought about a high degree of cohesiveness among members of the community.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: These familial and economic ties did not always work in favor of popular collective action. Disputes over water rights could flare up into open conflict between villagers and villages, while tenant farmers competed with one another to obtain tenancy rights as land became scarcer because of overall population growth. Thus, protestors employed a number of techniques to override such conflicting interests, as well as to prevent the free-rider problem in collective action. Some rural residents and villages were coerced into participating in the protest; others who refused to join were forced to make material contributions and were sometimes punished in the form of physical damage to their property (Imsullok, 29, 33). As observed in Japanese popular protests in the eighteenth century, and as argued by Herbert Bix, such coercive recruitment has been a ubiquitous feature of popular revolts throughout the world (Bix 1986, 74).

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: Despite the news that the provincial governor would order the abolition of the extra levy on households and the consolidated land tax, thousands of people, tying their foreheads with white cloths and holding wooden clubs, congregated in Ojukch’ŏn, a few miles away from the Chinju District seat, on the eighteenth day of the second lunar month; others gathered around the district office to protest. Magistrate Hong Pyŏngwŏn was terrified and sent a letter to Yi Myŏngyun to mediate the negotiation. Yi did come to rescue the magistrate and had Hong issue an official document guaranteeing that he would not institute the consolidated land tax, as the protestors demanded. A military officer named Kim Suman and others reportedly insulted and coerced the magistrate into issuing the document (Imsullok, 24; CCCT, 190–91; Chogyŏng kyerok, 5-6).

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: At any rate, the rebels called Yi “our commander” and even suggested erecting a commemorative stele for his merit (Imsullok, 32–33). Yi himself later insisted that he had intervened only because of Hongs request and that the rebels had shown him respect simply because he had not supported the consolidated land tax from the beginning. Yi thus denied his active role as the leader of the rebellion, maintaining that he had been framed by local clerks who hated him for his attitude of noninvolvement in local affairs (Yi Myŏngyun 1862).

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: The protest continued the next day, and this time the immediate targets were Military Commander Paek Naksin and his protégé. Though Hong Pyŏngwŏn had not done anything notably corrupt since becoming magistrate just before the rebellion, Paek was notorious for his corruption. For example, he lined his own pockets by tampering with the cash-grain conversion rate and then issued forced loans to make up for the lost funds. Paek made the people who had turned the Ch’ŏngch’ŏn training ground (which was under the care of the Military Commanders Office) into arable land and cultivated crops there for many years pay taxes suddenly, which apparently provoked resentment on the part of those cultivators. Paek also arbitrarily arrested wealthy people on the false charge of operating illegal mines in order to squeeze bribes from them (Imsullok, 7–9; CCCT, 189–90; Yongho hallok, 3:53–54).

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: To appease the angry protestors, Paek picked Kim Huisun, the clerk who had been accused of embezzling the most public funds, had him beaten to death, and then issued a document that rescinded the extra levy on households. Despite such conciliatory gestures, the protestors seized Paek and insulted him and kept him on the street for the whole night. Meanwhile, the rebels also killed another hated clerk, Kwŏn Ch’unbŏm, and threw Kims and Kwŏns bodies into the fire. Kwŏns son and his cousin, who had tried to save Kwŏn, were also beaten to death (Imsullok, 1, 13).

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: In the morning of the twentieth day of the month, the rebels went back to magistrate Hongs office and took him to where Paek was being held. After questioning and insulting, both Paek and Hong were eventually released. Their lives were saved, but their authority as centrally dispatched officials had been violated and denied by the people of the district. In contrast, rage against the local clerks, the symbols of administrative corruption, could not be restrained. In addition to Kim and the Kwŏns, Kim Yundu, the head clerk at the magistrates office, was caught trying to escape and was killed. Yi Kwijae, a firewood-gatherer, organized other protestors in chasing down and beating Kim Yundu to death (Imsullok, 24; CCCT, 190–91). On top of these attacks, the houses of corrupt clerks and local elite who had supported the consolidated land tax were demolished and burned (Imsullok, 1; Kyŏnam illok, 223).

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: Even in these outbreaks of violence, the victims were selected very carefully: Only those clerks who had been the object of popular resentment because of their history of unfair practices were attacked. Not all the clerks were corrupt. Some may have found it in their own best interests to collude with ordinary people in rent and tax relations, for they, too, experienced hardship in meeting tax quotas and resented the breakdown of the tax administration. In Chinju, Kim Wangmok, Sin Kapsŏn, and Cho Ijŏng, who worked for the district office, joined the rebel group (Imsullok, 29). Six administrative officials at both the magistrates and military commanders offices seemed to support the popular cause, for they were charged for not coming forward to protect their superiors (Imsullok, 35; Chogyŏng kyerok, 5).

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: The protests lasted for a few more days, and their activities included attacking rich and powerful households that had been notorious for their arbitrary exercise of power over villagers. Yi Samhyŏn (1807-?), the pacification commissioner of Right Kyŏngsang Province (Sŏnmusa), noticed during his pacification tour of Kyŏngsang that commoners (somin) insulted and attacked many yangban (taemin) because they had accumulated resentment toward the yangban elite for a long time. Although Yi did not know why the commoners hated the yangban, their anger certainly exploded during the widespread uprisings (Kyŏnam illok, 224, 226, 228). Indeed, the disorder and confusion unleashed by the popular movement liberated people from the constraints of normal life so that they could release their grievances and hatreds through violence. And with the feeling of new power and prestige granted to participants in the movement (no matter how temporary and superficial that feeling was), people were ready to act violently, particularly against their personal enemies. Villagers were extremely unhappy about the forced collection of interest on private loans, the use of private physical punishment, and the denial of access to mountains and hills to gather firewood. These grievances, combined with other problems about tax administration, led them to revolt and to exercise violence (Imsullok, 24).

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: Nonetheless, it seems that the rebels were selective in attacking the yangban or wealthy households rather than simply moved by uncontrolled rage. In Chinju, the houses of three people—the previous district commander, Mr. Chŏng; a lower civil service examination (chinsa) degree holder, Mr. Ch’oe; and a wealthy local yangban, Mr. Sŏng—were identified for burning by the rebels because these people had exploited the labor services of the local populace (Imsullok, 1). Kim Insŏp (1827–1903) of Tansŏng, a prominent yangban who had held the position of fourth censor in the Office of the Censor-General (Saganwŏn Chŏngŏn) but who had led an uprising there around the same time as the one in Chinju, noted that Sŏng from Namsŏng-ri, Ch’oe from Chŏnggang-ri, Cho from Sŏnam-ri, two Yis from Sawŏl-ri, and all others involved in the building of the private academy to honor Kim Sugŭn (1798–1854) of the Andong Kim descent group were attacked as well. They were targeted because they had supported the project to flatter the Andong Kim, the most powerful royal consort lineage at the time, and had forcefully mobilized labor for that cause (Tangye ilgi, 1861/6/17, 1862/2/23).

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: This aggression against a particular group of yangban may have been orchestrated by another group of local elite who opposed and criticized the establishment of a private academy for fraudulent political purposes. This incident, derived from intra-elite division, adds another complexity to the whole nature of the Chinju uprising.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: GOVERNMENT RESPONSESThe central government often showed a certain degree of compassion toward economically charged local disturbances that tended to die down spontaneously, without the mobilization of the military, when the government had promised to meet popular demands. In a Confucian state, the most important measure in ruling the people was to employ a morally respected man as magistrate. It was thought that when the magistrate was a morally perfect man, his benevolent rule would prevail over his people, and their lives would be harmonious and satisfactory. Consequently, the immoral nature of the magistrate and his misrule were immediately blamed when reports of the popular uprising in Chinju arrived at the central government on the twenty-ninth day of the second lunar month. Therefore, the first thing the government did was to fire the administrators there, namely, the magistrate Hong Pyŏngwŏn, Military Commander Paek Naksin, and Provincial Governor Kim Segyun (Imsullok, 19; Yŏngho hallok, 3:50).

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: In addition, the central government dispatched Pak Kyusu as special commissioner to investigate the local situation and to persuade and console the people. Pak Kyusu left for Chinju on the first day of the third lunar month and arrived there on the eighteenth. Pak was to look into administrative corruption by magistrates and clerks as the primary cause of the rebellion and to punish its leaders (Imsullok, 7).

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: It seems that he was moderate and cautious in his inquiries because he did not want to provoke more disturbances by taking strict measures in punishing the rebels (Imsullok, 22). Pak reported on Military Commander Paek Naksins corruption in the late third lunar month, and Paek was consequently banished to a remote island after inquisition and corporal punishment (Imsullok, 7–9; CCCT, 189–90). When Pacification Commissioner Yi Samhyŏn arrived in Chinju on the seventh day of the fifth lunar month, he urged Pak to wrap up his by then protracted investigation. Pak did so and quickly sent further reports to the central government (Kyŏnam illok, 213).

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: Paks recommendations for punishing the rebels were moderate. He divided them into five groups and recommended capital punishment for three ringleaders—Yu Kyech’un, Yi Kwijae, and Kim Suman—who were subsequently decapitated (Imsullok, 24–31). While Pak was in Chinju, he learned of the popular revolts in other districts and concluded that the primary responsibility for them lay with the educated local elite who had distributed circulars calling for local assemblies, which, in turn, provoked violent conflicts. In Chinju, Pak suspected that Yi Myŏngyun had been the key person. Though he could not find critical evidence to prosecute Yi, he recommended that the central government arrest Yi to further examine his role (Imsullok, 5, 23, 31-34). Yi was found guilty of involvement in the rebellion and was banished to an island. He was pardoned in about a year, but he died there before the news reached him (Imsullok, 36; Tangye ilgi, 1863/5/22).

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: Pak also examined the financial condition of the district and the Military Commanders Office, discovering various problems in the operation of the grain loan system that had been direct causes of the popular uprising in Chinju. In addition to urging temporary measures to relieve tax burdens in Chinju, he advised establishing a special office to review and discuss the general problems of tax administration and to devise solutions, which Pak thought should be tested in one province before being instituted in others (Imsullok, 15–18; CCCT, 177–78). This recommendation was taken after the central government became frustrated with continuous popular uprisings in the southern provinces, despite its efforts to soothe popular grievances, and realized that problems in tax administration were the fundamental cause of the rebellions.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: In fact, all the changes in tax administration at the local level did not seem to benefit the fiscal condition of the central government, although a group of privileged officials who routinely received bribes and kickbacks from their underlings may have enriched themselves.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: Thus, the state itself was also a victim of overgrown interest groups that extracted agrarian as well as commercial surpluses from the local tax system. On the twenty-fifth day of the fifth lunar month of 1862, King Ch’ŏlchong (r. 1850–63) ordered the establishment of the Three Administrations Reform Bureau (Samjŏng ijŏngch’ŏng) and informed his subjects that the court was about to launch a great reform (taegyŏngjang) plan. He asked all officials and scholars in the center and in the countryside to present reform ideas on the three tax administrations: land, military, and grain loan (Ijŏngchŏng tŭngnok, 302). After considering these proposals, the government announced reform policies on the nineteenth day of the intercalary eighth lunar month.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: These reform policies in general were intended to resolve the immediate problems that the people faced. Abolition of the consolidated land tax, prohibition of the illegal creation of new tax items, and strict application of a government-approved cash-grain commutation rate were adopted to rectify the land tax system. In the military tax system, the transfer of tax burdens to neighbors or relatives and illegal levies on children and the elderly were prohibited, following the original stipulations. More fundamental reforms were made in the grain loan system, which was to be abolished and replaced with a cash payment of 2 yang per kyŏl of land. These reforms were not revolutionary, in that they did not eliminate the roots of the problem, such as landlordism and taxation based on status distinctions. If carried out, however, they could have partially remedied those problems, for they would have reduced general tax burdens fell on rural population to a great extent.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: The ideas behind the reforms demonstrated the states ability to respond to changing social and economic conditions to a certain extent. Yet the policy package was abrogated about two months after the reforms were announced, and the untimely death of King Ch’ŏlchong the following year delayed further discussions on the matter.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: CONCLUSIONKim Yong (1805–65), a renowned yangban in Tansŏng, a district northwest of Chinju, had been accused of leading a tax riot in his home district in 1862 and was exiled to a remote island. Hearing the news about continuous uprisings in other districts of Kyŏngsang Province, Kim rhetorically wrote from his place of banishment, The people are Heaven. Can Heaven be deceived and overturned?” (Kanjŏng illok, 1863/1/16) This remark seems to endorse the idea of challenging a ruler when he does not behave like an upright one. Kim and his fellow yangban, such as Yi Myŏngyun of Chinju, were found guilty of launching such challenges.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: Still, the rural elite—such as Kim Yongs son, Kim Insŏp—went farther, for they perceived exploitative magistrates and their subordinate clerks as thieves and enemies who were ruining peoples livelihoods and thus be driven out (Tangye ilgi, 1862/2/4 and 1862/2/15). They saw their own actions as attempts to remove those evil practices and elements from local administrations, and thus they felt no regret about taking matters into their own hands. Indeed, they strongly resented allegations against them by the central court because they were convinced that their demands—whether in the form of peaceful legal measures or aggressive struggles—for the rectification of corrupt tax administration, which had wreaked such havoc on the rural economy, were ideologically justified. Precisely because the popular protests of 1862 progressed within such ideological confines, they never developed into an antistate movement.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: On the surface, the purpose of the popular movement was to resist arbitrary and abusive taxation, which could not be accepted any longer by rural population. This economic struggle was also a political one, as the rural elite felt, not without reason, that their dominant power and authority in local society had been seriously compromised. Not only had they become the primary prey of the newly devised extra levies, but also their routine control over tax distribution and collection had been denied. In traditional Korea, the state, the social and economic elite, and the general population adjusted to changing social and economic conditions while jockeying for control over the nations limited resources. But the introduction of a monetary economy and the subsequent expansion of commerce and trade produced new economic opportunities that were most effectively tapped by local clerks, who learned how to manipulate monetized market and the tax system long before the state figured out how to put its hands on it. When the damage to the rural economy caused by malfeasance in tax administration became too great to absorb—and the legal means to solve the problem did not show any hope of rectifying the clerks corrupt practices—the people leaned toward violent struggle.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: The processes and courses taken by local elite leaders and protestors unmistakably reveal the deep divisions and competition that had built up in local society. Frictions that had developed along class, social status, community, and political lines resulted in different patterns of protest in what started as a tax riot. Rural institutions such as lineage associations and village compacts, which reflected familial, communal, and cultural interests and tied rural communities together, also had a decisive impact on popular political behaviors. Thus, despite polarization of the class structure between landownership and land cultivation, the pauperization of people of every status group did not automatically foment the sort of class consciousness that might have led to class-based conflict. Rather, the emphasis on the hereditary nature of social status—accompanied by long-standing ideological justification and cultural practices—rationalized the local elites power and authority over limited resources and mitigated class-based antagonism. As a result, the tax-resistance movement was initiated primarily by the rural economic elite, who were most affected by the ever-increasing arbitrary taxation and who could no longer bear their authority slipping out of their hands. Ordinary people were then mobilized through various rural networks, such as kinship, village, and interest associations, to fill the rank and file of the movement.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: Once violence erupted, however, other preexisting contentious relations contributed to the spread of aggression. Oppressive rural strongmen were punished. Those who had politically defied specific cultural traditions upheld in the area were also penalized. No doubt personal grudges were involved in certain cases of hostility, but as we have seen, most of those targeted were carefully selected on economic or political grounds. Examination of the specific context of local history and society should therefore allow us to understand the complex nature of this social conflict.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: Also interesting is the spatial limitation evident both in the Chinju uprising and in protests in other districts. The nature of certain tax structures confined the struggle within the boundaries of a given district, although the news of a tax riot in a nearby district did encourage neighboring districts experiencing similar grievances to rise up in protest themselves. But the main reason that a multidistrict united front either did not appear or was temporary and tenuous when formed is that the tax system was managed on the basis of local administrative units, and each unit had different customs, regulations, and problems, even though the roots of all the problems were basically institutional and statewide. Moreover, the cultivators were scattered and managed their parcels independently under a system of smallholdings, making it difficult to lay the foundation for a class alliance. Finally, the protesters primary goals were to lighten or abolish unjust taxes and to remove corrupt administrators in the local power structure rather than to overthrow the existing rule (including rural class relations). Thus, there was no basis for a wider political organization that could have made a countrywide movement out of the individual uprisings with respect to either political or religious organizations. Because the goal of the 1862 rebellions was to obtain the immediate redress of local problems, the protesters voluntarily dispersed, before military intervention, when the magistrate or special commissioners agreed to carry out the reforms they had demanded. This absence of revolutionary sentiment in the demands of an ordinary rural population can also be witnessed in traditional popular protest movements in other parts of the world.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: The nineteenth century in Korean history is often called the age of rebellions because a number of major rebellions—beginning with a more politically charged rebellion in the northwestern region in 1812, followed by the rebellions in 1862, and reaching a peak by the Tonghak rebellions of 1894–95—punctuated stable dynastic rule that had lasted for more than four hundred years. Did these events, especially the first two major ones, represent the decline of dynastic rule? They did not immediately bring about the fall of the dynastic structure, for the dynasty continued until 1910. This seems to testify to the relative strength of the Chosŏn state and its adaptability to changing environments. Although the central court was unable to carry out fundamental institutional changes that might have rooted out problems in the tax system, its immediate responses to the rural demands, no matter how short-sighted they were, was effective enough to rule out the development of locally confined revolts into an antidynastic movement.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: In understanding of the causes and processes of the 1862 popular rebellions in Chosŏn Korea, this study argues that previous paradigms, such as the theories of dynastic decline and class struggle, explain only a part of the whole. The former accurately indicates the maladministration of taxation by corrupt officials as the immediate cause of the rural unrest, but it does not discuss how larger social and economic changes derived from the expansion of commerce and the introduction of monetary economy in the late Chosŏn period created complicated problems that should not be simply labeled administrative corruption. Violent struggles motivated by class antagonism did emerge in the latter stages of the Chinju uprising, but acute class consciousness was not the prime cause of the popular movements at this time. The existence of class antagonism in rural Chosŏn cannot be denied because of extremely unequal distribution of land and wealth. Nonetheless, this study argues that other rural relations based on kinship and villages tended to suppress class-based contention.

author: Sun Joo Kim
essay_title: Taxes the Local Elite and the Rural Populance in the Chinju Uprising of 1862
essay_text: The 1862 rebellion in Chinju resembles popular uprisings in Qing China and Tokugawa Japan in a number of ways. Undoubtedly no rebellion is the same as any other, but a comparative look at similar events does enhance our understanding of popular political behaviors under specific conditions. Each study mentioned in this work tends to emphasize one or more aspects of rural society, such as moral economy, rational choice, local politics, elite leadership, the availability of preexisting networks for mass mobilization and organization in rural contention, and agency of the state and officials representing the state. This study finds that all these elements were important in making this rebellion, although each element played a different role in the processes of the rebellion. The history of Chinju society and its popular movements certainly conforms to some aspects of conventional rural agrarian society and culture. Nevertheless, because the trajectories of each episode are extremely complex, we need to view them through the lens of its particular historical context and avail ourselves of eclectic theoretical approaches.

author: John Lee
essay_title: The Rise of the Brokered State - Situating Administrative Expansion of Choson Korea
essay_text: It can be agreed that the Choson Dynasty (1392–1910) was remarkable for its longevity. Assessment of the dynastys lifespan, however, runs into a morass of historiographical contention. Japanese colonial-era scholars such as Fukuda Tokuzō depicted the Choson era as one of socio-economic stagnation that left Korea underdeveloped and unprepared for the modern world. In the 1960s and 1970s, the South Korean internal development school of Kim Yongsop unearthed an array of changing social dynamics in late Choson society that highlighted social upheaval, progress, and “sprouts of capitalism.” In North America, James Palais characterized the Choson order as an “aristocratic-bureaucratic balance,” that is, a ruling elite marked by hereditary ascription but additionally defined by service in the central bureaucracy. By limiting the entrance of political newcomers and checking royal power, this aristo-bureaucratic hybrid, Palais argues, maintained Chosons “remarkable stability without the application of major structural reforms.

author: John Lee
essay_title: The Rise of the Brokered State - Situating Administrative Expansion of Choson Korea
essay_text: While these aforementioned arguments may differ wildly in their conclusions, they share a commitment to static archetypes that implicate modalities of progress, stagnation, or modernization in Korean history. Rather than inserting Korea into teleological constructs or predetermined theories, this article situates the Choson era in the longue durée dynamics of historical change on the Korean Peninsula itself, within the long-term processes of centralization, administrative expansion, and local transformations.

author: John Lee
essay_title: The Rise of the Brokered State - Situating Administrative Expansion of Choson Korea
essay_text: In the previous article of this theme issue, Javier Cha explains the formation of a centralized aristocracy in the Koryo Dynasty (918–1392). The early Choson state was built upon the patrimonial structures and centripetal forces described by Cha. Aristocratic coalitions in Seoul, bound by conjugal ties and shared participation in civil examinations and the bureaucracy, accelerated ongoing patterns of centralization on the Korean Peninsula. Fifteenth-century reformers established new administrative subdivisions, bestowed provincial governors with higher status and far-ranging powers, and revamped the land system in favor of greater access for members of the central bureaucracy. Simultaneously, Choson bureaucrats embarked on an ambitious program of political and cultural reform, targeting everything from the role of the king and officials to the content of national customs (kuksok 國俗) and the position of women.

author: John Lee
essay_title: The Rise of the Brokered State - Situating Administrative Expansion of Choson Korea
essay_text: The rise of this particular blend of bureaucratic and cultural order, however, required a departure from previous trends in Korean history. The process of administrative expansion eventually produced a vast array of brokers—intermediaries who could fulfill the logistical demands of state. Policies necessitated implementation; ideas needed articulation; resources required identification, extraction, and distribution. From the sixteenth century onward, the infrastructural capacities of the Choson state flowed through a wide range of local elites, middlemen, administrators, and soldiers who managed and intermediated increasingly complex links between Seoul and the provinces.

author: John Lee
essay_title: The Rise of the Brokered State - Situating Administrative Expansion of Choson Korea
essay_text: I refer to this post-1500 trend as the rise of the brokered state. By “state,” I mean not only the capital-based government (the court, the central bureaucracy, and the capital-based military) but also the wider administrative apparatus represented by magistrates, clerks, and military officials in the countryside. Together, the central government and local administrators fit Max Webers definition of the state as that human community which (successfully) lays claim to the monopoly of legitimate physical violence within a certain territory. Moreover, the Choson bureaucracy served as a mechanism for what Pierre Bourdieu refers to as “the symbolic violence over a definite territory. By instilling the need for proper” rituals and correct gender roles, establishing “orthodox interpretations of scholarship, and demarcating jurisdictional authority over key resources and their distribution, the Choson state realized itself not just through the king and his ministers but also in the social and mental structures, intellectual pursuits, and broader aspirations of the yangban elite that multiplied in the provinces over the course of the dynasty.

author: John Lee
essay_title: The Rise of the Brokered State - Situating Administrative Expansion of Choson Korea
essay_text: I use the term brokered state to further distinguish the mid-to-late Choson era from the patrimonial centralization of Koreas medieval period. Historical sociologist Charles Tilly used the term “patrimonialism” to define the tribute and feudal levy-based regimes that predominated in Europe until the fifteenth century. Tilly then applied the term “brokerage to describe the subsequent period between roughly 1400 to 1700 in important parts of Europe when rulers relied heavily on formally independent capitalists for loans, for management of revenue-producing enterprises, and for installation and collection of taxes. The transition from patrimonial to brokered states was tantamount to European state formation—a process, according to Tilly, made possible by the changing stakes of war. The medieval pattern of patrimonial extraction transitioned to territorialized brokerage as “closely administered territories became assets worth fighting for, since only such a territory provided the revenues to sustain armed force.”

author: John Lee
essay_title: The Rise of the Brokered State - Situating Administrative Expansion of Choson Korea
essay_text: The Choson context was somewhat different from cases described in classic historical-sociological literature in which western Europe, China, and Japan are the primary referents. Choson had no feudal legacy. Unlike China and the Japanese archipelago, local warlordism was not an issue on the Korean Peninsula after 1000 CE. While merchants and financiers became the primary brokers of state capacity in parts of western Europe, Choson administrative expansion relied far more on the activities of lower-level clerks, military officials, and most importantly, official and nonofficial elites from the yangban stratum. State formation on the Korean Peninsula between 1400 and 1800 was not the by-product of wartime finance or the challenges of local warlords. Rather, the Choson state can be seen as a broadening assemblage of center-local interactions that developed gradually in response to infrastructural and political limits apparent from 1500 CE onward.

author: John Lee
essay_title: The Rise of the Brokered State - Situating Administrative Expansion of Choson Korea
essay_text: With such historical differences in mind, the vocabularies of patrimonialism and brokerage remain useful. Karen Barkey reinterpreted Tillys concepts in the context of the early modern Ottoman Empire to produce an exemplary study of how the Ottoman state incorporated bandits and other potentially uncooperative elements into the bureaucracy. Scholars of late imperial China, likewise, have meticulously detailed how imperial officials and local elites collaborated to broker state interests, developing what Prasenjit Duara calls a “cultural nexus of power through which the imperial state could use various channels—temples, market networks, kinship groups, patron-client relationships—to reach into local communities.

author: John Lee
essay_title: The Rise of the Brokered State - Situating Administrative Expansion of Choson Korea
essay_text: Amidst the unreliable infrastructure and incomplete information that bedeviled pre-industrial Eurasia, middlemen and intermediaries were essential tools of governance. Research on societies as disparate as ancient Egypt, the Roman Empire, and early modern France has highlighted the critical role played by local elites, tribal chieftains, tax farmers, and military garrisons in cementing central rule and facilitating the wider dissemination of goods and information. The vast array of intermediaries between the central and the local formed the basis for a state infrastructure, to use Philip Gorskis term, across early modern Eurasia, akin to “a communications network through which information flows between the central and the local or as a generator that feeds additional power to the state.

author: John Lee
essay_title: The Rise of the Brokered State - Situating Administrative Expansion of Choson Korea
essay_text: South Korean historiography likewise has highlighted the rise of local and regional elites, particularly elements of the so-called sarim faction in the sixteenth century, as a key turning point away from the centralizing tendencies of the dynastys founding elites. Economic historians of Korea have put forth detailed studies of the middlemen brokers such as the merchants who facilitated the expansion of the late Choson economy. However, such studies have been largely descriptive: at most, they highlight the brokers role in the functioning of a larger political or fiscal system. I argue that the broker in the Choson era was not simply a cog in a web of state institutions—he constituted the very matter of the web that was the Choson state. Local elites disseminated, articulated, and practiced the dominant cultural ethos, notably Confucianism, and rendered them synonymous with the Choson cultural order and the states very legitimacy. Clerks, military officials, and tribute merchants distributed the resources that underpinned the states revenue and security. The array of brokers who arose in the Choson Dynasty after the mid-sixteenth century distinguish the era and inscribe it in a longue durée pattern between the medieval patrimonialism described by Javier Cha and the post-1860 reformist administrations laid out by Holly Stephens.

author: John Lee
essay_title: The Rise of the Brokered State - Situating Administrative Expansion of Choson Korea
essay_text: What Choson experienced between the early sixteenth and nineteenth centuries was not decentralization. The state did not lose control.” Rather, brokered interactions between center and local changed and reshaped the nature of the state. The mechanisms of developing and imposing political, social, and economic norms required the involvement of various elements that had not been nearly as significant or robust before the sixteenth century. The brokered state gradually arose after the turmoil of Yonsanguns reign (1494–1506) and peaked around 1800 after a century of increasing stability, population growth, and cultural and economic efflorescence, an era that built much of the popular imagination of what constitutes “traditional Korea. Culturally and ideologically, the Choson era was when Confucian beliefs and practices gradually permeated the Korean Peninsula. At the institutional level, brokered administration became the Choson states modus operandi, its mechanism for expansion and its basis for enduring stability.

author: John Lee
essay_title: The Rise of the Brokered State - Situating Administrative Expansion of Choson Korea
essay_text: Both South Korean and international research on Choson Korea in the past three decades has produced a rich corpus of local histories and empirical institutional studies. These, along with my own primary research on Choson-era forest management, will serve as the basis for the following argument. The rise of the brokered state between the early sixteenth and nineteenth centuries can be observed in four salient trends: one, the rise of local elites as key cultural and economic brokers in the sixteenth century; two, the growing role of local status-group, academic, and kinship organizations; three, the expanding functions of clerks and local military garrisons; and four, the increasing role that local brokers played in managing resources meant for state use (kugyong 國用) after 1600. The rise of local elites in the sixteenth century engendered a symbiotic relationship between themselves and the government. Local elites required state sanction to maintain their status and privileges; the state required local elite assistance to rule the country. After the devastating Imjin War (1592–1598) and Manchu incursions of 1627 and 1636, the government utilized clerks, military officials, and similar local bureaucratic organs to reassert control over a devastated countryside. Thus, the brokered state was the effect of a two-tiered process beginning with the mounting prominence of elites in the mid-sixteenth century and intensifying after 1600 as a widening array of military officials, clerks, and other lower-level officials brokered the links between capital and countryside.

author: John Lee
essay_title: The Rise of the Brokered State - Situating Administrative Expansion of Choson Korea
essay_text: Local Elites and the Sixteenth-century ShiftIn his magnum opus, Confucian Statecraft and Korean Institutions: Yu Hyongwon and the late Choson Dynasty, James Palais described sixteenth-century Korea as a time of political and social “disintegration,” an era when the high-minded reformism that had launched the dynasty degenerated into maladministration [and] internecine bureaucratic factionalism, and Choson society became beset with what Palais calls “negative trends—the concentration of wealth, the evasion of responsibility, and the deterioration of national defense. Only the devastating Hideyoshi invasions at the end of the century, attests Palais, gave the Choson Dynasty a chance to rebuild.

author: John Lee
essay_title: The Rise of the Brokered State - Situating Administrative Expansion of Choson Korea
essay_text: Negative perceptions of the sixteenth century in Korean historiography dwell on the failed promises of early Choson statecraft. The reformist dreams of fifteenth-century scholars, in Palais view, fell into the quagmire of elite self-interest and irresponsibility. Some South Korean scholars such as Kim Sõngu have similarly portrayed the sixteenth century as a dismal period in Korean history when political turmoil, administrative corruption, and the end of government support for irrigation facilities led to economic decline in areas such as Sõnsan County in Kyongsang Province.

author: John Lee
essay_title: The Rise of the Brokered State - Situating Administrative Expansion of Choson Korea
essay_text: Other historians, however, have noted that the sixteenth century also coincided with periods of economic growth and the expansion of a key group: local elites. Kim Sõngu himself notes that, even while Sõnsan declined in the sixteenth century, upland areas of Kyongsang Province such as Yean grew in wealth and stature. The spread of rice transplantation and small-scale irrigation techniques helped support an increasingly confident rural elite in parts of southeastern Korea. Yean, for instance, grew into a prominent town, home to Neo-Confucian scholar Yi Hwang (1501–1570) and an assertive scholarly culture that regularly saw local literati insert themselves in central politics through the dissemination of joint memorials.

author: John Lee
essay_title: The Rise of the Brokered State - Situating Administrative Expansion of Choson Korea
essay_text: The localization thesis, that local elite consolidation from the mid-sixteenth century onward had profound implications for the Choson Dynasty, is part of Martina Deuchlers longue durée study of the Choson ascriptive elite. Anchored in kinship-centered descent groups and further defined by shared participation in ritual and scholarly affairs, the Choson elite, the sajok, were able to maintain their socio-political dominance until the end of the Choson Dynasty. Their dominance of central politics can be traced to the fifteenth century, and in the case of some illustrious families further back to even the Koryo and Silla eras. Elite ascendancy in the countryside, however, required a localizing transition from the fifteenth through the sixteenth centuries, when established kinship groups reclaimed land and brought tax-burdened small cultivators under their protection (often as bonded slaves). By 1600,” writes Deuchler, the sajok controlled the countryside.

author: John Lee
essay_title: The Rise of the Brokered State - Situating Administrative Expansion of Choson Korea
essay_text: By the mid-seventeenth century, local elites had emerged as the primary intermediary transmitting Confucian culture between state and locality. Many understood themselves as local grand officers” (hyang taebu 鄉大夫) tasked with the role of “rectifying the local mores” and protecting the communitys moral reputation. Hwisang Cho argues that local elites further consolidated their dominance by using certain textual practices, notably epistolary interactions and the penning of joint memorials, to simultaneously access a sense of participation in central politics and solidify a network of Confucian elites within a given locality. Such were the benefits of brokerage: in linking center and local to serve the states interests, local elites also served their own.

author: John Lee
essay_title: The Rise of the Brokered State - Situating Administrative Expansion of Choson Korea
essay_text: Accordingly, local elites also became key engines of economic growth, particularly through the method with the best marginal returns in the early Choson era: land reclamation. Yi Sugon and Kim Köntae have touted the sixteenth century as an era when local elites furthered their role in agricultural development, especially in the southern provinces of Cholla, Kyongsang, and Chungchŏng. According to their line of argument, local elites emerged in areas where land and labor were available to claim and where reliable water supplies facilitated the spread of wet-rice cultivation. The process was indeed, in Martina Deuchlers words, a “land grab.

author: John Lee
essay_title: The Rise of the Brokered State - Situating Administrative Expansion of Choson Korea
essay_text: Government policy further incentivized the agricultural expansion that underlay the dominance of the yangban stratum in the provinces. Reclamation rights were encoded in the Great Code of Administration (Kyŏngguk taejon): “If one has laid out and occupied a field for three years, the occupier then possesses the land. John Richards characterizes such property laws—the rights to occupy, alienate, mortgage, and bequeath lands so owned—as “common to settled societies in [early modern] Eurasia.” State sanction and the solidification of usage rights drove the clearing and cultivating of the frontier throughout the pre-industrial world, and Korea was no different in following this pattern.

author: John Lee
essay_title: The Rise of the Brokered State - Situating Administrative Expansion of Choson Korea
essay_text: It is important to note that state sanction was key. Local elites required close cooperation with the state to acknowledge property rights and acquire resources; the state, in turn, required cooperation to govern the countryside and extract taxes, tribute, and corvée labor. Kim Sõngu has argued that reductions in government support for dikes and irrigation caused agricultural productivity to fall in some areas in the early sixteenth century. While central support for local activities may have diminished, local elites were often able to fill the vacuum, in turn enriching their own patrimonies. Elite “localization in this period, writes Deuchler, meant the appropriation of a particular locale as economic basis for maintaining, through continued examination success and/or marital ties, relations to the center.

author: John Lee
essay_title: The Rise of the Brokered State - Situating Administrative Expansion of Choson Korea
essay_text: In the next two sections, I use two case studies to peer further into the rise of local elites in the sixteenth century. In the first, I examine how one prominent yangban in Cholla Province collaborated with state officials to acquire construction material for himself and his kin. In the second case, I shed light on another yangban from Kyongsang province who utilized his position to assist the states tribute collection system while also enriching himself. Together, the cases reflect the symbiotic relationship between Choson local elites and the wider state. The state could not function without local elites acting as cultural and economic brokers; likewise, local elites depended on state recognition of their privileges in order to protect their interests.

author: John Lee
essay_title: The Rise of the Brokered State - Situating Administrative Expansion of Choson Korea
